2051274428630143028.text:
I gave Codex one idea:

A screen-time app for kids that doesn’t feel like a punishment.

Then it helped turn that idea into Peekaboo, a gentle mobile app built around a tiny purple character with a sprout on its head. 🌱

The workflow was wild:
🎨 GPT Image 2.0 shaped the cozy visual world, mascot poses, sticker rewards, and app-store-style mockups
🧠 GPT-5.5 helped design the product logic: timers, breaks, rewards, parent moments, and kid-friendly microcopy
📱 Codex pulled it together into an interactive mobile app prototype with real screens, transitions, animations, and state

Prompt below 👇

2051274432119701625.name: Bas Fijneman
2051274432119701625.text:
I used @givros his awesome prompt to get this to life! 

I want to recreate the Peekaboo mobile app — a gentle screen time app for kids.

The app must feel soft, calm, and emotionally safe. Every interaction should feel reassuring rather than punishing. The character (Peekaboo, a small purple blob with a sprout on its head) is the emotional anchor of the app.

The app must reproduce a satisfying, gentle mobile interaction system.

The UI must feel tactile, soft, and reassuring to navigate.

Screen layout:
- Render the app inside a phone frame mockup at 375x812 (iPhone 14 size).
- Use a safe area with a status bar at the top showing time, signal, wifi, battery.
- Place a fixed tab bar at the bottom with 4 tabs: Home, Timer, Rewards, Profile.
- Active tab uses the brand purple, inactive tabs use a soft muted gray.
- Each screen has its own scrollable content area between status bar and tab bar.
- Content should never touch the edges. Use generous 20px horizontal padding.

Idle state:
- The Peekaboo character has a subtle breathing animation (gentle scale 1.0 to 1.02 and back).
- Soft ambient elements drift slowly (clouds, sparkles, leaves).
- Cards and panels sit at rest with a soft drop shadow.
- All animations use easing, never linear motion.

Press state:
- When a button is pressed, it scales down to 0.96.
- Background color darkens slightly.
- Release returns to scale 1.0 with a gentle spring (overshoot to 1.02 then settle).
- Buttons must feel like soft silicone, not glass.

Swipe/scroll state:
- Vertical scroll has a soft rubber-band overscroll.
- Horizontal swipes between screens feel weighted and decelerate naturally.
- Scroll position must never feel jittery or instant.

Tab transition:
- Tapping a tab cross-fades content with a small upward slide (12px).
- The active tab indicator slides between positions, not teleports.
- Character poses can change between screens with a soft fade.

Animation:
- All movements must be smooth.
- Do not snap or teleport elements.
- Use interpolation for position, opacity, and scale.
- Use spring physics for press/release feedback.
- Character animations loop seamlessly.

Suggested UI element states:
- idle
- pressed
- active
- disabled
- success

Required screens:

1. Home screen
- Greeting at top: "Good morning, Alex!" with a small sun icon and date.
- Settings gear icon in the top right.
- Large rounded card showing "Today's screen time" with "1h 15m left of 2h 30m" and a circular progress ring around an illustration of Peekaboo sitting in grass with clouds and a sun.
- Streak banner at the bottom: "You're on a roll! 5 day streak" with a flame icon and chevron.

2. Timer screen
- Encouragement message at top: "Keep it up, Alex!" with a small heart.
- Large circular progress ring with the time remaining ("15:00 minutes left") in the center.
- Peekaboo character below, waving.
- "15 more minutes of fun!" pill button.
- Pause button and sound toggle at the bottom.

3. Break screen (when time is up)
- "All done! Time to take a break." headline.
- Peekaboo holding a wooden sign that says "Time to play outside!"
- Decorative stars and sparkles around the scene.
- Yellow pill button: "5 more minutes — Ask a parent" (with a lock icon).
- Green pill button: "I'm done! See you tomorrow!"

4. Rewards screen
- "Nice job, Alex!" with "You're doing amazing." subtitle.
- Weekly streak card with 7 day circles (M T W T F S S), filled stars for completed days.
- Sticker earned card: "You earned a sticker! Gardener Peekaboo" with the character holding a flowerpot and trowel.
- Unlocked rewards section with a progress bar (2 of 5) and 5 reward icon tiles in a row.

The final result should feel like a polished, production-quality kids app:
soft greetings, warm illustrations, gentle progress tracking, and reassuring micro-interactions.

Visual inspiration:
Use peekaboo_reference.png as the primary visual reference for layout and tone.

Also use the following art direction as inspiration:

Create high-quality hand-painted Ghibli-inspired mobile app assets for a cozy children's screen time app.

Character:
Peekaboo is a small, round, purple blob creature with a tiny green sprout growing from the top of its head. It has soft rosy cheeks, big black expressive eyes, and small stubby arms. The character should feel adorable, calm, gentle, and friendly. Never scary, never overstimulating. The character should feel emotionally safe for a 5-10 year old child.

Multiple poses needed:
- Sitting in grass, idle, with a soft smile
- Standing and waving with one arm raised
- Holding a wooden sign reading "Time to play outside!"
- Gardener pose, holding a small flowerpot with a trowel
- Celebration pose with arms up

Environment:
Soft pastoral backdrops painted in watercolor and gouache. Gentle hills, fluffy clouds, small flowers, soft grass, dappled afternoon sunlight. The world feels like a quiet sunlit afternoon in a Ghibli film. Add subtle bloom, soft fog, and floating particles for warmth.

App UI:
Render a polished cozy mobile app interface:
- a soft cream and lavender background
- rounded cards with subtle shadows
- generous whitespace and soft typography
- a clear bottom tab bar with 4 sections
- pill-shaped primary buttons
- circular progress rings with soft gradient strokes
- gentle iconography (home, timer, star, profile, settings, sound, pause, lock, heart, flame, sun)

Important:
All interface text must be in English.
Use short, friendly, encouraging labels such as:
- "Good morning"
- "Today's screen time"
- "Keep it up"
- "Time to play outside"
- "Nice job"
- "5 day streak"
- "You earned a sticker"
- "Unlocked rewards"
- "5 more minutes"
- "I'm done"

Avoid corporate, clinical, or stern wording. Tone is warm, gentle, never scolding.

Art style:
Hand-painted Ghibli-soft 2D illustration, watercolor and gouache textures, gentle ink outlines, polished cozy mobile app UI, dreamy storybook atmosphere, soft cinematic afternoon lighting, expressive character animation, and a premium app store feature look.
Use clean rounded shapes, clear readable silhouettes, soft shading, and a charming nostalgic visual style.
The design should feel more like a polished animated picture book than a painted illustration.
Use a warm pastel palette: cream, butter yellow, soft lavender purple, sage green, dusty rose, and sky blue accents.
The overall feeling should be cozy, gentle, magical, encouraging, and emotionally safe for children.

Composition:
9:16 portrait phone format for individual screens.
Phone-frame mockup composition for the marketing landing view.
Keep all UI clearly visible and within safe areas.
Make each screen feel like a polished feature shot from a cozy kids app.

Development requirements:
Develop the app using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Split the project into as many files as needed to keep it modular, clean, and easy to improve.

The project must include an Assets folder.

Important asset rule:
Use only images placed inside the Assets folder.
Do not create visual assets with CSS shapes, emojis, SVG placeholders, or external images.
All visual assets must come from images generated with GPT Image 2.0.

Required assets to create with GPT Image 2.0:
- 1 app background (soft gradient with floating clouds, leaves, stars)
- 1 Peekaboo character — sitting in grass, idle pose
- 1 Peekaboo character — standing, waving
- 1 Peekaboo character — holding "Time to play outside!" sign
- 1 Peekaboo character — gardener with flowerpot
- 5 reward sticker icons (paint palette, book, cupcake, magnifying glass, gift)
- 1 set of tab bar icons (home, timer, star, profile)

Asset generation rule:
Each character pose and each sticker must be generated one by one.
Each must be a separate transparent PNG file.
Do not create a single sprite sheet.
Do not generate multiple poses in one image.
Each image must be usable independently in the app.

Playable demo requirements:
The demo must work directly by launching index.html.

The demo must include:
- A working bottom tab bar that switches between 4 screens.
- A live countdown timer on the Timer screen that updates every second.
- A circular progress ring that animates as time passes.
- Working press/release animations on all buttons.
- Animated character idle breathing on every screen.
- Smooth screen transitions between tabs.
- A streak display that reads from a small JSON config.
- A reward unlock progress bar.
- A modal or screen change when the timer completes (Break screen).
- Soft sound effects on button press (optional, mutable).
- Persistent state in localStorage (current screen time, streak, unlocked stickers).

Behavior:
- Tapping "15 more minutes of fun!" extends the timer by 15 minutes.
- Tapping "5 more minutes — Ask a parent" requires a 4-digit parent PIN modal.
- Tapping "I'm done!" returns to the Home screen with a celebration animation.
- The character pose changes contextually per screen.
- Decorative ambient elements (clouds, sparkles) drift slowly in the background.

Files:
Organize the code clearly, for example:
- index.html
- css/style.css
- css/animations.css
- js/main.js
- js/Router.js
- js/TimerManager.js
- js/StreakManager.js
- js/RewardManager.js
- js/CharacterAnimator.js
- js/StorageManager.js
- js/components/TabBar.js
- js/components/ProgressRing.js
- js/components/Button.js
- js/components/Modal.js
- js/screens/HomeScreen.js
- js/screens/TimerScreen.js
- js/screens/BreakScreen.js
- js/screens/RewardsScreen.js
- Assets/background.png
- Assets/peekaboo_idle.png
- Assets/peekaboo_waving.png
- Assets/peekaboo_sign.png
- Assets/peekaboo_gardener.png
- Assets/sticker_paint.png
- Assets/sticker_book.png
- Assets/sticker_cupcake.png
- Assets/sticker_search.png
- Assets/sticker_gift.png
- Assets/icon_home.png
- Assets/icon_timer.png
- Assets/icon_star.png
- Assets/icon_profile.png

The final result must respect the cozy Ghibli-soft Peekaboo theme and the gentle visual atmosphere described above.
Every label, message, and button in the UI must be written in English.
Tone must remain warm, encouraging, and never punishing.

2114511681707475416.name: Jeremy Hillsberg
2114511681707475416.text:
October 25, 2026

Day 16 of building what I hope will become the most important app for human health ever created.

It's Sunday evening, and I made some progress over the weekend, although not quite as much as I'd hoped.

I still haven't tested the entire app yet.

I've had a bunch of things to take care of around the house, and I haven't been able to dedicate the time needed to sit down, go through every workflow, and make sure everything functions and looks the way I want it to.

That's probably going to happen next weekend.

I did get a few things accomplished this weekend.

First, I designed the app icon.

I spent some time looking for good tools and workflows for creating an iOS app icon, but couldn't find anything particularly helpful.

So I ended up putting together my own process.

I had ChatGPT generate a very detailed image generation prompt, which I then passed into Google's Nano Banana image model.

After a few iterations, I got something I really liked.

I downloaded the image, imported it into Figma using my free account, adjusted the dimensions, zoomed in slightly to make the central icon more prominent, and exported it in the proper format for iOS.

Then I added it to the app. I'll attach a preview to this post. Let me know what you think!

The next thing I did was have Claude Code redesign the app's UI to match the color scheme and visual identity of the new icon.

No longer surprisingly, it managed to do that in one shot.

It showed me mockups of every page, gave me a few options, and updated the overall design.

I haven't gone through everything in detail yet, so I'm sure there will be adjustments, but the initial results look really good.

It also created light, dark, and tinted versions of the app's appearance.

I'm not entirely sure how necessary all three are, but it's nice to have the options.

Another thing I've started thinking about is optimizing the app for Apple's new iPhone Duo.

I've been seeing quite a bit of feedback from people reviewing the device, and one common complaint seems to be that very few apps are actually optimized for it.

My hope is that Apple will favor apps that take advantage of the new form factor.

I found a skill someone shared on X that might help with that process, but I'm going to save it for later.

First, I need to make sure the app actually works properly on a standard iPhone.

Then I'll worry about optimizing it for additional devices.

One other thing I'm working on that I'm pretty excited about is a public GitHub repository documenting everything I'm learning throughout this process.

It won't contain any of my app's source code.

Instead, it'll be a collection of workflows, prompts, best practices, lessons learned, and useful resources from building an iOS app with AI.

The interesting part is how I'm structuring it.

I'm designing the repository specifically so that someone can point a general-purpose AI agent or coding agent directly at it.

The agent will be able to navigate the repository, understand what's available, and pull in the specific instructions or resources it needs.

For example, if someone wants to create an iOS app icon, the repository will contain the exact workflow I followed, the prompts I used, and the best practices I learned along the way.

I'll keep adding to it as I work through development, testing, App Store submission, and everything else that comes up.

It's still in the early stages, and I have quite a bit to add before I'm ready to share it publicly.

But eventually, I'd love for it to become a useful resource for anyone trying to build an iOS app with AI, especially people who have never done it before.

So that's where things stand after 16 days.

The initial application is built.

The app icon is finished.

The UI has been redesigned around the new visual identity.

And I'm starting to document everything I've learned in a way that other people and AI agents can actually use.

The big remaining question is whether the app works as well as Claude Code thinks it does.

Hopefully I'll have an answer to that next weekend.

For now, I'm looking forward to Sunday Night Football.

Should be a good game.

🧶 to follow…

How to Build Fr€€ AI Voice Agents with Google Gemini — and Monetize Them 👇👇

Step 1: Design the "Brain"

Before doing anything else, your AI needs a distinct personality and operational logic. Head to Gemini and use it to craft your instructions.

Type this prompt:

"Help me create a system prompt for an AI voice agent for [Your Business Name]. It needs to handle client inquiries about [Your Core Services], outline our pricing, maintain a [Desired Tone] tone, and know how to handle common objections like [Insert Objection]."

Goal: Gemini will output a polished behavioral script. Copy this text—you will need it for the next step.

Step 2: Configure the Voice Agent

Now, set up your logic engine.

➔ Go to Google AI Studio and sign in.

➔ In the sidebar, click "Build" and select "Create conversational voice apps."

➔ Paste the behavioral script from Step 1 into the "System Instructions" box.

➔ Select Gemini Flash as your model. It is the best choice because it prioritizes the speed required for natural, real-time voice conversations.

Hit Generate.

➔ Crucial Step: Test it! Click the microphone icon and speak to it. If the greeting sounds clunky, type a correction (e.g., "Make sure you always ask for their phone number before ending the call"). The model updates instantly.

Step 3: Generate the Website Interface

Now, we use AI to build the website that houses your voice agent.

➔ In Google AI Studio, stay in the "Build" workspace.

➔ In the prompt or instructions area, type this request:

"Generate the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code for a modern, professional landing page for [Your Business Name]. The page should include a prominent, integrated voice interaction button that connects directly to this AI voice agent's functionality so users can speak to it immediately."

➔ Visualize: Click the "Run" or "Preview" button in AI Studio. The system will generate the code and a visual representation of your landing page, fully integrated with your voice agent.

Step 4: Deploy & Go Live

You don't need to pay for expensive hosting.

➔ For a professional site, host it for free on GitHub Pages or Vercel.

➔ Simply copy the code generated in Step 3, paste it into an index.html file, and upload it to your chosen platform to get a live, public URL that you can send to any business owner in the world.

Step 5: How to Monetize

The technology is powerful, but the business model is what actually pays.

The Pitch: "I can build you a 24/7 AI voice receptionist that captures leads, answers FAQs, and books appointments while you sleep."

The Strategy:

➔ Pick a Niche: Focus on a specific local business (e.g., a gym, dental clinic, or real estate agency).

➔ Build the Demo: Create a fully functional, custom-tailored demo for that specific business before you even contact them.

➔ The "Proof" Outreach: Send them the live URL and invite them to call it.

➔ Close the Deal: Show them the math. Every missed after-hours call is a lost lead that your AI can now capture, qualify, and book.

2114433316925657165.name: Real Alpha
2114433316925657165.text:
Choosing the right task matters more than adding compute

Diogo Almeida on The TWIML AI Podcast with Sam Charrington. Almeida is co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe, which released Jev as a model for bringing intelligence into software. Before TypeSafe, he spent four and a half years at OpenAI, working on efforts including InstructGPT and RLHF, after earlier work at Google.

Almeida argues that text-generating models are poorly suited to many software tasks because those tasks require structured, reliable decisions rather than human-readable strings. He describes Jev and RLCD as an effort to make calibrated intelligence available to software developers, with probabilities that let builders set their own policies. He says useful AI should be one component in an engineered system, not a single model asked to do everything. The discussion also considers how reliable decision models could change agent design and when businesses should choose engineered workflows over flexible but less reliable automation.

Minute by minute

1. Automation needs decision-shaped models (1:53)
Sam asks why agents struggle with basic data entry and insurance underwriting despite excelling at some research and coding tasks. Almeida says current systems center on transformers optimized to produce text, while accounting and similar work require discrete decisions meant for computers.

2. The task directs ML progress (8:02)
Almeida reframes the bitter lesson. He argues that choosing the right task matters more than compute, and that data must be gathered for that task. He says RLHF required creating a new kind of human-feedback data from scratch, and that finding the right direction can lead to major advances.

3. Demos still fall short of automation (12:25)
Almeida says he moved from Google to OpenAI, where he spent four and a half years on several projects, while remaining focused on why AI struggles with easy work. He argues that demos can look like science fiction without supporting dependable background use, and that some products fall back to human review. He points to Waymo as an engineering-led example and says ML should be scoped within a larger system.

4. Jev targets machine-native intelligence (21:08)
Almeida says Jev grew from his longstanding goal of optimizing intelligence for software automation rather than strings. He describes classifiers as useful interfaces for putting intelligence into software, not as an innovation in themselves, and says Jev aims to give developers flexible capabilities without assembling a specialist team.

5. Reliability matters more than cheap inference (27:13)
Almeida says speed and cost are not the core advance. Developers are paying for intelligence, and a model only delivers what it was optimized to do. He says Jev's supporters recognized the value of structured outputs and programmatic use, and that TypeSafe has kept a high reliability bar even when it slows releases.

6. Building calibrated intelligence was hard (32:19)
Almeida says he initially thought the work would take a week, but producing robust, calibrated decisions required extensive work on model weaknesses and task design. He argues that developers need to operate at a useful semantic level rather than maintain many narrow cases, and describes Jev as a set of building blocks for intelligence applications.

7. Jev recombines existing model weights (39:05)
Almeida says Jev uses multiple open-weight models with different trade-offs and a process he considers more than conventional post-training. The field does not yet have a settled term for it. He says TypeSafe focuses on the intended task and removes elements tied to string generation, rather than pretraining from scratch, which he sees as resource-intensive for the gains.

8. Calibrated probabilities give builders control (46:03)
Almeida defines RLCD as a family of algorithms aimed at calibrated decisions, with probabilities that let developers apply their own policies in code. He argues builders should be able to set thresholds for actions such as refusing or escalating, rather than rely on inconsistent model choices or instructions in a system prompt.

9. Post-training can warp probabilities (54:04)
Almeida says the underlying models are more calibrated than RLHF and RLVR models, which he argues can distort probabilities in order to generate strings well. He says a calibrated-decision objective can build on models' existing capabilities to improve calibration and reliability.

10. Generalization depends on the objective (59:02)
Almeida questions whether decision tasks should be presumed harder to generalize than text, arguing that familiarity and the long tail of examples affect what appears out of distribution. He says ChatGPT already felt general for many tasks, while distinguishing generality from reliability on a particular workflow.

11. Training objectives shape generality (1:03:05)
Almeida argues that RLVR can intensify benchmark-shaped jaggedness, while RLHF was relatively easy to generalize because it optimized for subjective, human-pleasing responses. He says generality may be harder under RLCD and harder still under RLVR, while describing Jev as an early release that he expects to improve on business workflows.

12. Code should carry application logic (1:08:20)
Almeida speculates that better training data, rather than an agent loop alone, may explain improvements in coding agents, while noting he is reasoning from outside the labs. He argues that Jev should be called from users' code instead of relying on a universal harness, with builders supplying the application logic.

13. Agents could escape KV-cache constraints (1:16:25)
Almeida says TypeSafe wants to help agent builders make systems more reliable and efficient, though his team is not expert in identifying agent use cases. He argues that agents' append-only KV caches constrain routing, tool calls and flexible state, and imagines cheap, reliable intelligence enabling more selective context and control.

14. Rigid workflows suit repeat automation (1:22:20)
Almeida says one-off tasks may suit flexible, imperfect LLMs, but valuable background workflows justify engineered code and reliability. He sees being on rails as a feature for automation and expects hybrid systems that combine models with software workflows. For TypeSafe's next steps, he mentions additional models, early access and hiring.

The link in the reply plays each point from its second.

Prompt:

 [BRAND NAME]
Act as a High-End CGI Product Photographer and 3D Render Artist
specializing in streetwear merch and limited-edition collectibles.

PHASE 1: CONCEPT & OBJECT

Create a photorealistic CGI product shot of a premium keychain set
suspended in mid-air against a neutral gradient studio background.
The keychain set consists of THREE elements connected to a single
polished silver carabiner clip with a gold-plated split ring:

ELEMENT 1 — ACRYLIC TAG:

A rectangular acrylic charm (approx. 4:9 ratio, rounded corners, 3mm thick).
Layered construction: clear gloss acrylic front panel over a [BRAND NAME]-colored
background insert. The background insert carries bold, condensed all-caps
typography — autonomously generate a short poetic or brand-relevant phrase
(4–8 words) that matches [BRAND NAME]'s tone of voice, set in a heavy
condensed grotesque typeface (Bebas Neue / Impact / custom bold). Include
[BRAND NAME]'s URL or tagline in small print at the bottom of the insert.
Micro-printed fine text fills the lower third as a design texture element.

ELEMENT 2 — OVAL MEDALLION CHARM:

A die-cut oval hoop/ring shape (donut silhouette, 40mm diameter) made from
tinted translucent acrylic or resin. Autonomously determine the iconic
brand color of [BRAND NAME] and apply it as the tint (deep saturated,
jewel-tone translucency — e.g., gold, cobalt, emerald, crimson).
The [BRAND NAME] wordmark is engraved or UV-printed in bold all-caps
along the inner curve of the ring. Add 1–2 small iconographic symbols
(logo mark, globe icon, cloud glyph) laser-engraved onto the face.
Subtle radial sun-ray pattern embossed on the surface.

ELEMENT 3 — HARDWARE:

Silver anodized aluminum carabiner with knurled locking barrel.
Gold-plated brass split ring (key ring loop) at the top.
All metal surfaces show micro-scratches and machining marks —
no perfect CGI plastic. Industrial precision aesthetic.

PHASE 2: MATERIAL & TEXTURE

Render all acrylic elements with full Ray Tracing and Subsurface
Scattering — light must visibly pass through the tinted acrylic
creating internal glow. Apply Fresnel reflection on acrylic edges.
Surface imperfections: hairline scratches, micro-dust particles,
smudge traces on the clear panel (subtle, editorial-level — not dirty).
Metal: PBR metallic workflow — anisotropic specular highlights on
the carabiner barrel, brushed finish on the ring.
Typography on acrylic must appear screen-printed or UV spot-coated —
slight ink texture, not floating.

PHASE 3: COMPOSITION & STAGING

Levitation shot: the entire keychain set hangs suspended from the
top of frame, centered with a 10–15 degree rotation to the right
(showing dimensionality). Nothing touches a surface — pure float.
Camera angle: slightly below eye-level looking up at ~5 degrees,
portrait orientation (4:5 ratio).
Depth of Field: focus plane centered on the oval medallion,
acrylic tag in sharp secondary focus, top hardware with micro
bokeh blur. Aperture equivalent: f/4.0.
Negative space: generous — object occupies 55% of frame.

PHASE 4: LIGHTING

Primary: large octabox soft key light, positioned top-right at
45 degrees — creates clean specular bloom on acrylic edges.
Secondary: subtle rim light from bottom-left, cool temperature
(5500K), separates the object from background.
Background: seamless gradient cyclorama — dark steel blue (#1a2535)
at top transitioning to pale silver-grey (#d0d8e0) at bottom.
No hard shadows cast. Global Illumination active.
Chromatic Aberration: micro-level, visible only on acrylic edges
(adds realism, prevents CGI-plastic look).
No lens flare. No neon. No HDR overblown highlights.

TECH SPECS

Render engine: Octane Render or Blender Cycles (path-traced)
Resolution: 4096 x 5120px (4:5 portrait)
Samples: 4096 minimum
Color profile: Adobe RGB, D65 white point
Post-processing: subtle film grain overlay (ISO 400 equivalent),
+5 clarity, -10 highlights, neutral color grade
Output mood: High-end streetwear lookbook / limited drop product page
Style references: Kith accessories, Highsnobiety product editorial,
Fragment Design merch photography
NEGATIVE: No white studio infinity cove. No flat lay. No hand holding
the product. No fake bokeh blur filters. No AI plastic sheen.
No floating text outside the object.

---------------------------------

指令：基于附带的照片，将图像显示在复古手机的屏幕界面内，并进行特定的风格变换。

画面描述：这是一张抓拍的、略微倾斜的复古诺基亚手机特写（经典直板造型，例如 6610 或类似的早期彩屏机型），手机在画面中随意地呈对角线放置。低分辨率的发光 LCD 屏幕占据了构图的主导地位，填满了大部分视野。周围坚固的塑料外壳和物理 T9 键盘/导航键的顶部区域仅部分可见，并在画面边缘被裁剪掉。

屏幕内容：像素化的屏幕上显示着一个实时的“相机预览”界面：

照片内容： 附带照片中的人物经过转换，身穿明显的千禧年 Y2K 流行时装（例如闪亮的金属面料、天鹅绒运动装、水钻细节或层叠网眼织物）。整个场景呈现出浓重的早期拍照手机美学：明显的像素网格（纱窗效应）、有限且略微褪色的调色板，以及块状的压缩伪影。

复古 UI 叠加： 覆盖在照片视图之上的是低像素、单色的诺基亚用户界面元素。 屏幕顶部边缘：像素化的信号强度条（左）、“Camera”文字（中）、块状电池图标（右）。 屏幕底部角落：块状像素字体的软键（Soft-key）标签，左侧显示“Options”（选项），右侧显示“Back”（返回）。
氛围与光影：屏幕发出特有的绿蓝色 LCD 背光色调，微弱的光线投射在周围的塑料边框上。整体氛围怀旧、具有互动感，且呈现出真实的低保真（Lo-fi）科技感。
参数设置：

比例： 4:5 竖幅

相机视角： 复古手机屏幕微距特写，手持视角

屏幕模拟： 早期 CSTN 或 TFT LCD 屏幕，可见像素颗粒，特有的绿色色偏
UI 元素： 复古低分辨率单色像素图标和块状文字覆盖
内容变换： 将人物服装替换为 Y2K 千禧年流行风格
调色风格： 低饱和度冷色调，数字噪点，颜色抖动伪影，屏幕荧光

Byebye Alex Xu, hello 🍌nano banano pro with “Infographic” prompt

(Just kidding! I’m actually a big fan of Alex Xu’s posts. I trust his work—unlike AI, which can have hallucinations and produce incorrect results or diagrams.)

1. Send the prompt below to Gemini, along with the content you want to turn into an infographic. ( or create a Gem with the prompt to reuse it)

2. Gemini will generate a structured description of the infographic based on your input.

3. In the same session, ask Gemini to draw it using Nano Banana Pro. (Alternatively, if you aren't using Gemini directly, simply copy the generated text into Nano Banana Pro).

Example conversation：https://t.co/RyIhMzqJdh

----

Pompt:

----

You are A WORLD-CLASS INSTRUCTIONAL DESIGNER.

You are a master of creating clear, concise, and engaging learning materials. You are also an expert in visual design, and you know how to use visuals to communicate complex ideas in a way that is easy to understand. You are also a master of storytelling, and you know how to use stories to make learning more memorable and engaging.

Your task is to analyze the provided Source Context and User Steering Prompt and generate a structured Infographic Content that informs an expert infographic designer what has to be conveyed so that the viewer clearly understands the source context.

This will be passed to an expert infographic designer in the next step who will rely on it to create a high quality infographic. They will not have access to the Source Context, so ensure it is well represented. The infographic must be in the same language as input or English.

You will also analyze the provided User Steering Prompt and extract only the design-related instructions (style, layout, color, etc.) into a dedicated Design Instructions section at the end.

THE PROCESS

Step 1: Analyze the source document.
Read the whole document and develop a deep understanding of its content.

Step 2: Create a high-level outline.
The outline should include a title and a list of all the main learning objectives.

Step 3: Flesh out the outline.
For each learning objective, create a section. Each section will have a mix of conceptual explanations and practical, hands-on tutorials.

CRITICAL RULES

Rule 1: Output format is Markdown.
All generated content must strictly adhere to Markdown formatting.

Rule 2: Tone and voice.
The tone should be that of an expert trainer: knowledgeable, encouraging, and clear.

Rule 3: No new information.
Do not add any information that is not present in the source document.

Rule 4: Handling of source data.
All data from the source document MUST be copied verbatim. Do not summarize or rephrase.

THEY GAVE YOU THEIR EMAIL BECAUSE YOU PROMISED HELP.

SO WHY ARE YOU ONLY SENDING THEM SALES PITCHES? 📩

Someone discovers your business through Google.

They read your article.

They like what you teach.

They download your free guide.

They give you permission to send helpful emails.

Then what happens?

Maybe they receive an automatic confirmation.

Then silence.

Or worse, an endless stream of unrelated promotions.

Here's the missed opportunity:

They were interested enough to give you their email.

They just weren't ready to buy.

What if your Grok Bot could turn that first spark of interest into a helpful relationship that leads naturally toward a sale?

Not through pressure.

Not through spam.

But by delivering the right information, to the right subscriber, at a useful time.

Today, we're teaching your Grok Bot SEO team to build an INTELLIGENT EMAIL MARKETING ENGINE. 🧠

One that educates, builds trust, answers buying objections, presents useful offers, and knows when to stop.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 STEP 1: UNDERSTAND WHAT EMAIL MARKETING SHOULD ACCOMPLISH

Remember post #18?

We built a system that captures leads, sends confirmations, and routes inquiries.

That was the response system.

This is the relationship-building system.

A person downloading your free guide isn't necessarily asking to speak with a salesperson.

They may want to understand a problem.

Learn a useful skill.

Compare solutions.

Or decide whether they need your service at all.

Your next email should help them take the next useful step.

Here's the journey we're building:

<escape>👋 WELCOME</escape>

Deliver what the subscriber requested.

↓

💡 TEACH

Help them solve a small problem.

↓

🏆 BUILD TRUST

Provide a demonstration, genuine example, or useful insight.

↓

❓ ANSWER OBJECTIONS

Explain the important questions that may prevent a buying decision.

↓

🎁 PRESENT AN OFFER

Introduce a relevant product or service when appropriate.

↓

✅ ADAPT OR STOP

Change the sequence when someone purchases, requests help, changes preferences, or unsubscribes.

Each email should earn its place in the subscriber's inbox.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 STEP 2: STOP SENDING EVERYONE THE SAME MESSAGE

Imagine you're running a digital marketing agency.

One subscriber wants help improving Google rankings.

Another wants a chatbot.

Another needs automated lead follow-up.

And another is comparing CRM software.

Should they all receive the same email series?

Probably not.

This is called SEGMENTATION.

Segmentation means grouping subscribers by relevant interests, needs, or behavior.

For example:

🔎 SEO INTEREST

Receives useful lessons about search visibility, website improvements, and qualified traffic.

🤖 AUTOMATION INTEREST

Receives demonstrations of lead capture, booking systems, and customer follow-up.

📊 COMPARING SOLUTIONS

Receives explanations of available services, packages, pricing, and differences.

💳 EXISTING CUSTOMERS

Receive the fulfillment, training, and support messages relevant to their purchase.

Any additional promotional email should follow their communication preferences.

Your Grok Bot can help build different paths without creating a new Bot for each audience.

Use information subscribers voluntarily provide and legitimate business records.

Don't guess sensitive personal facts or invent buying intentions.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 STEP 3: CREATE EMAILS PEOPLE ACTUALLY WANT TO OPEN

Let's make these more interesting than:

"Check out our latest blog post."

Or:

"Buy now before it's too late."

Teach Buyer Voice to write seven types of emails.

1️⃣ THE QUICK WIN

Subject example:

"One small website fix that may save lost inquiries"

Give the reader one useful improvement they can make today.

2️⃣ THE LIGHTBULB MOMENT

Subject example:

"Your traffic problem might actually be an offer problem"

Challenge a common assumption.

Explain the missing insight.

3️⃣ THE VERIFIED NEWS STORY

Subject example:

"What this week's AI announcement means for small businesses"

Use an actual event, verified sources, and a practical lesson.

4️⃣ THE CONTRARIAN TAKE

Subject example:

"More leads won't fix a broken booking process"

Explain why a popular strategy sometimes fails.

Offer a better approach.

5️⃣ THE GENUINE SUCCESS STORY

Subject example:

"What changed after this business simplified its booking process"

Use a verified result, demonstration, or clearly labeled hypothetical example.

6️⃣ THE OBJECTION ANSWER

Subject example:

"Do you actually need expensive software to automate customer follow-up?"

Answer a question that prevents someone from making a decision.

7️⃣ THE RELEVANT OFFER

Subject example:

"Want us to build the follow-up system for you?"

Explain what is included, who it helps, the real price, and the next step.

Use only approved promotions and genuine deadlines.

Notice the difference?

Some emails teach.

Some surprise.

Some help people make decisions.

And some introduce an offer.

The sequence should feel like useful guidance, not a sales pitch chopped into seven pieces.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🗓️ STEP 4: BUILD A USEFUL WELCOME SEQUENCE

Here's an example for someone who requested a guide about getting more customers online.

📩 EMAIL 1 — WELCOME

Suggested timing: Immediately after confirmed enrollment.

Deliver the requested guide.

Explain what the subscriber will learn.

Make the next step simple.

📩 EMAIL 2 — FIRST USEFUL WIN

Suggested timing: Day 2.

Teach one practical improvement.

Show exactly how to apply it.

📩 EMAIL 3 — SURPRISING INSIGHT

Suggested timing: Day 4.

Explain a common marketing mistake.

Show what to do instead.

📩 EMAIL 4 — PROOF OR COMPARISON

Suggested timing: Day 7.

Provide a real demonstration, useful comparison, or verified example.

📩 EMAIL 5 — ANSWER AN OBJECTION

Suggested timing: Day 10.

Address a common concern about time, cost, complexity, or results.

📩 EMAIL 6 — THE RELEVANT OFFER

Suggested timing: Day 14.

Introduce the approved solution.

Explain who it's for and what's included.

Give the reader one clear next step.

These are example intervals, not universal rules.

Your Bot should adapt the number of emails and timing to the actual business and subscribers.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🤖 STEP 5: USE YOUR EXISTING GROK BOT TEAM

Open your SEO Operations group chat from post #14.

We'll use four specialists.

👑 SEO LEAD

Coordinates the email strategy.

Reviews the approved offer.

Approves the plan for implementation.

💬 BUYER VOICE

Writes persuasive subject lines, stories, explanations, and offers.

📊 KEYWORD & DATA

Reviews subscriber interests, clicks, customer actions, and campaign results.

🛠️ WEBSITE & CONTENT

Builds the email sequences, segments, automation rules, links, and tracking.

No additional Bots required.

And here's an important way to save Grok Bot usage.

Your email platform sends the emails.

Your Grok Bots build, test, and improve the system.

Your Bots don't need to run every hour just to check which email comes next.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📋 STEP 6: COPY THIS PROMPT INTO YOUR GROK BOT TEAM

📌 COPY FROM HERE:

"@SEO Lead, coordinate an INTELLIGENT EMAIL MARKETING & CUSTOMER NURTURING CAMPAIGN for [BUSINESS NAME].

Website: [WEBSITE URL]

Email marketing platform: [PLATFORM / UNKNOWN]

CRM: [PLATFORM / UNKNOWN]

Primary approved offer: [OFFER]

Main goal: [QUALIFIED LEADS / BOOKINGS / SALES / OTHER]

Our goal is to build an automated, permission-based email system that gives subscribers useful information, builds trust, answers relevant buying questions, and introduces appropriate offers.

Use our existing:

• SEO Business Brief.

• Buyer Voice research.

• Approved Offer & Sales Funnel Report.

• Lead-to-Revenue Automation System.

• Search-to-Sale Scoreboard.

• Buyer Interest & Content Engine.

Assign email writing and editorial strategy to Buyer Voice.

Assign segmentation research and performance tracking to Keyword & Data.

Assign campaign setup and implementation to Website & Content.

SEO Lead will coordinate the work and approvals.

🔍 1. AUDIT OUR EXISTING EMAIL MARKETING SYSTEM

Inspect our authorized email platform.

Identify:

• Existing lists or contact segments.

• Email subscription forms.

• Where each subscriber came from, if recorded.

• Available marketing permission records.

• Existing campaigns.

• Active email sequences.

• Contact tags.

• Existing workflow triggers.

• Follow-up schedules.

• Current suppression rules.

• Unsubscribe handling.

• Sending-domain setup.

• Existing campaign performance.

Create a simple email-system map.

Reuse our lead capture and confirmation system from post #18.

Do not recreate existing working automations.

🎯 2. DEFINE THE SUBSCRIBER JOURNEYS

Identify up to FOUR useful subscriber groups based on available information.

Examples:

A. New subscribers requesting a free resource.

B. Subscribers interested in a specific service.

C. Prospects comparing products or packages.

D. Existing customers who have agreed to receive relevant additional marketing.

For each group, identify:

• How they entered the list.

• What they requested.

• What they may reasonably want to learn.

• Relevant known interests.

• Main questions.

• Suitable content.

• Appropriate next action.

• Communication preferences.

• Conditions for leaving the sequence.

Keep necessary account or order emails separate from optional marketing.

❤️ 3. FIND THEIR BIGGEST QUESTIONS AND OBJECTIONS

Reuse our Buyer Voice research.

Identify the FIVE most important questions or buying objections supported by the research.

Consider:

• Price.

• Time required.

• Difficulty.

• Trust.

• Product suitability.

• Alternatives.

• Delivery expectations.

• Expected value.

• Customer responsibilities.

For each objection, explain:

A. What the subscriber may be worried about.

B. What we know from genuine customer evidence.

C. What information could help them decide.

D. Which approved offer or resource is relevant.

Do not manufacture emotional fears or objections unsupported by our research.

🧠 4. DESIGN THE EMAIL LEARNING JOURNEY

Build a sequence that progresses logically.

Use this structure where appropriate:

WELCOME → QUICK WIN → NEW INSIGHT → PROOF → OBJECTION ANSWER → OFFER.

Adapt the structure for different customer needs.

Every email should give the subscriber a reason to read it.

Avoid repeating the same benefit in slightly different words.

Do not add emails just to increase the sequence length.

✍️ 5. WRITE SIX COMPLETE WELCOME & NURTURE EMAILS

For EACH email, provide:

Internal email name.

Intended subscriber group.

Trigger or scheduled delay.

Main purpose.

THREE subject-line options.

One short preview-text option.

Complete email body.

Useful link or resource.

One primary call to action.

Required personalization fields.

Exit or suppression conditions.

Any claim requiring verification.

Preview text is the short text that may appear beside the subject line in an email inbox.

Write conversationally.

Use short sentences.

Explain unfamiliar terms.

Keep paragraphs easy to scan.

Use engaging openings without fake urgency.

Make the subject line accurately reflect the message.

Each email must offer a meaningful insight, answer, demonstration, or next step.

Keep the writing as short as the topic allows.

📰 6. CREATE A TIMELY STORY EMAIL SYSTEM

Use the verified research process from our Buyer Interest & Content Engine.

Find up to THREE relevant current stories or recent developments.

For each, record:

• Original source.

• Event date.

• Publication date.

• Supporting evidence.

• Why our subscribers may care.

• The useful lesson.

• What they can do with it.

• The relevant business resource, if any.

Write ONE complete educational newsletter using the strongest supported topic.

Create:

• Three subject lines.

• Preview text.

• Opening hook.

• Short news summary.

• Practical business lesson.

• Actionable next step.

• Appropriate link or CTA.

Do not imply that a public figure or company endorses our business.

If no timely story meets our standards, use a relevant evergreen customer question instead.

💡 7. CREATE A LIGHTBULB EMAIL

Choose one belief our ideal buyer may misunderstand.

Use actual evidence to explain the issue.

Write an email that:

• Opens with a surprising but accurate idea.

• Explains the common mistake.

• Shows why it matters.

• Offers a practical correction.

• Connects to an existing educational resource.

The goal is to improve the reader's understanding.

Not to provoke controversy merely to attract clicks.

🎁 8. CREATE AN OFFER EMAIL

Use our approved offer from post #17.

Write ONE complete sales email.

Include:

• Who the offer helps.

• The problem it addresses.

• The desired result.

• Exact included components.

• Relevant quantities or limits.

• Delivery process.

• Verified proof, where available.

• Approved price or pricing destination.

• Real terms and conditions.

• Main CTA.

If the offer has an actual promotion, use its verified terms and expiration date.

Do not invent scarcity, countdowns, earnings claims, or guarantees.

Provide two different opening hooks for testing.

🌳 9. BUILD THE SUBSCRIBER PATHS

Use the existing email platform's native automation features.

Create appropriate paths based on reliable information.

Examples:

NEW RESOURCE SUBSCRIBER

Deliver the requested material.

Begin the relevant educational sequence when marketing enrollment is authorized.

SUBSCRIBER INTERESTED IN A SPECIFIC TOPIC

Use a relevant interest tag or subscriber-selected preference.

Send appropriate educational content.

PROSPECT REQUESTING SALES ASSISTANCE

Route the inquiry through the approved lead-response workflow.

Avoid sending repetitive sales messages.

CUSTOMER WHO PURCHASED

Stop prospect promotions that no longer apply.

Use the correct customer delivery or onboarding process.

MARKETING OPT-OUT

Stop marketing messages.

Respect the subscriber's preference across applicable campaigns.

Use verified status changes and existing platform tools.

Email-link clicks may provide useful signals, but automated security tools can sometimes create false clicks.

Do not make consequential assumptions based only on one recorded click.

🔁 10. SET EMAIL FREQUENCY & STOPPING RULES

Recommend a sensible schedule based on the customer journey.

Configure:

• Delays between emails.

• Maximum relevant campaign frequency.

• Suppression of duplicate messages.

• Conditions for ending a sequence.

• Purchase and booking exits.

• Valid opt-out handling.

• Failed-address handling.

• Routing for relevant customer replies.

Use subscriber preferences where supported.

Avoid enrolling one contact in several overlapping promotional sequences.

If someone requests to stop marketing emails, honor that request.

Do not treat a purchase as permission for unrelated promotional campaigns.

📨 11. VERIFY EMAIL DELIVERABILITY

Inspect our authorized sending platform and domain setup.

Verify appropriate email authentication.

Include:

• SPF.

• DKIM.

• DMARC.

These are methods that help email providers verify the sender.

Check our actual platform's current requirements.

Also verify:

• Sender name.

• Working reply-to address.

• Valid physical mailing address in commercial emails.

• Unsubscribe function.

• Required one-click unsubscribe support.

• Mobile formatting.

• Working links.

• Accessible images and alt text where appropriate.

• Relevant email consent records.

Use an approved postal mailing address.

Do not publish a private home address unnecessarily when a legally acceptable alternative is available.

Follow the applicable laws and current provider requirements for our audience.

If technical access is available, prepare supported authentication fixes and request authorization for consequential changes.

🔗 12. CONNECT EMAIL TRAFFIC TO BUSINESS RESULTS

Use consistent campaign tracking links.

For example:

utm_source=newsletter

utm_medium=email

utm_campaign=welcome_series

Use additional tracking labels when useful.

Connect the links to the correct landing pages.

Do not place subscriber names, email addresses, or sensitive contact information in tracking URLs.

Where supported, measure:

• Delivered messages.

• Clicks.

• Relevant website visits.

• Qualified inquiries.

• Bookings.

• Purchases.

• Unsubscribes.

• Spam complaints.

• Revenue linked to campaigns when reliable.

Treat email open rates cautiously because privacy and automated email systems can make them unreliable.

📦 13. BUILD THE CAMPAIGNS INSIDE OUR PLATFORM

Use our existing authorized email marketing account.

Where supported:

• Create contact segments.

• Set up relevant tags.

• Create email campaigns.

• Add approved email drafts.

• Configure delays.

• Create conditional workflow paths.

• Set stopping rules.

• Connect relevant forms.

• Configure appropriate tracking.

• Prepare the newsletter.

• Connect the correct sales pages.

Use draft or non-sending states until final approval.

Use native email automation rather than scheduling Grok Bot to send each message individually.

If the current platform cannot support a requested feature, document the actual limitation and a suitable alternative.

🧪 14. TEST THE ENTIRE EMAIL JOURNEY

Use clearly identified test contacts.

Test:

A. New eligible subscriber enrollment.

B. Welcome email delivery.

C. Correct sequence order.

D. Relevant content links.

E. Mobile email display.

F. Subscriber interest tagging.

G. Available branching rules.

H. Relevant replies.

I. Purchase or booking exit.

J. Marketing opt-out.

K. Suppression of duplicate messages.

L. Tracking links and conversion events.

M. Correct handling of failed email delivery.

Verify actual behavior.

Correct confirmed failures.

Repeat affected tests.

Do not send the live campaign to the full audience as a test.

🛑 15. REQUEST OWNER APPROVAL

Prepare one approval package.

Include:

• Subscriber groups.

• Subscription and permission rules.

• Complete email copy.

• Subject lines.

• Schedule.

• Offer links.

• Any promotions.

• Workflow map.

• Tests completed.

• Potential costs.

• Stop conditions.

• Reporting plan.

Request approval before enabling live marketing campaigns or making material changes to customer communications.

Record the approved scope.

🚀 16. ACTIVATE THE APPROVED CAMPAIGNS

After authorization, use the email platform to activate the approved sequences.

Verify:

• Correct audience.

• Correct sender.

• Correct enrollment triggers.

• Correct email order.

• Correct delays.

• Working unsubscribe controls.

• Active stopping rules.

• Accurate campaign status.

Record the activation date.

If the sender domain has little or no sending history, recommend a gradual rollout suited to platform guidance.

Do not suddenly send a large campaign to an unverified or stale list.

📊 17. MEASURE CUSTOMER VALUE

Create an EMAIL MARKETING PERFORMANCE REPORT.

Record:

• Number of eligible subscribers.

• Messages sent and delivered.

• Delivery failures.

• Click rates.

• Relevant page visits.

• Qualified leads.

• Bookings.

• Purchases.

• Revenue, where reliably attributed.

• Unsubscribes.

• Spam complaints.

• Performance by subscriber group.

Compare results against meaningful business goals.

Separate initial data from established patterns.

Do not treat an opened email as proof of genuine customer interest.

🏆 18. IMPROVE THE STRONGEST EMAILS

Identify the messages that appear to help subscribers take useful actions.

Consider:

• Subject line clarity.

• Value of the lesson.

• Relevance to the subscriber.

• Quality of the resource.

• CTA wording.

• Landing page quality.

• Timing.

• Email frequency.

Recommend up to THREE practical tests.

Use sufficient data before declaring a winner.

Don't change every variable at once.

Preserve successful educational content.

Improve weak messages that serve an important purpose.

Remove unnecessary emails that provide little value.

💰 19. KEEP GROK BOT USAGE EFFICIENT

Use our existing Bots.

Reuse verified customer and content research.

Create related emails in one production batch.

Use native email platform triggers and delays.

Use existing reports for measurement.

Avoid unnecessary Bot-to-Bot chatter.

Do not run an AI Bot every few minutes to check whether emails need sending.

After successful implementation, offer to save the process as a Skill called:

INTELLIGENT EMAIL MARKETING ENGINE.

Recommend one narrow weekly Routine only if recurring analysis adds useful value.

For example:

'Every Monday, review the previous week's authorized email marketing reports.

Identify delivery failures, important unsubscribe problems, and meaningful changes in qualified leads or sales.

Recommend up to three improvements.

Do not send new campaigns or change live communication rules without approval.'

Use native platform alerts for issues requiring faster attention.

📁 20. DELIVER THE COMPLETE IMPLEMENTATION PACKAGE

Create:

INTELLIGENT EMAIL MARKETING ENGINE - [BUSINESS NAME]

Include:

Existing system audit.

Subscriber groups.

Buyer questions and objections.

Email journey map.

Six complete nurture emails.

Subject lines and preview text.

One verified timely newsletter.

One lightbulb email.

One approved-offer email draft.

Segmentation and tagging rules.

Schedule and stopping rules.

Sending-domain status.

Tracking configuration.

Campaigns created.

Test results.

Approved activation status.

Initial performance report.

Recommended improvements.

Reusable Skill instructions.

Remaining owner decisions.

Complete all authorized implementation work.

Provide links to the finished campaigns where available.

Deliver one combined report.

Stop after completing the approved assignment."

✅ END OF PROMPT.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚀 STEP 7: SEE WHAT A USEFUL EMAIL CAN LOOK LIKE

Imagine someone downloads your free guide about marketing automation.

A few days later, they receive this email.

SUBJECT: You might not need more website traffic.

"Most business owners want more people visiting their website.

The email taught something useful.

Created a lightbulb moment.

And introduced a relevant service without making the entire email a sales pitch.

That's the kind of email worth receiving.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚡ STEP 8: MAKE THE SYSTEM SMARTER WITHOUT MAKING IT MORE EXPENSIVE

Here's the part that can save you a significant amount of unnecessary Bot activity.

Your Grok Bot creates the email system ONCE.

Your email platform then handles:

✅ New subscriber enrollment.

✅ Scheduled email delivery.

✅ Appropriate interest tags.

✅ Conditional paths.

✅ Purchase-related exits.

✅ Unsubscribe handling.

✅ Supported campaign tracking.

Your Grok Bot returns when an actual review, improvement, or new campaign is needed.

The system doesn't need an AI Bot running around the clock to work.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌱 STEP 9: ADAPT THE CAMPAIGN TO YOUR BUSINESS

FOR DIGITAL MARKETING AGENCIES

Teach subscribers how to improve websites, lead capture, bookings, and customer follow-up.

Introduce approved service packages when relevant.

FOR PLANT-BASED BUSINESSES

Share recipes, useful product information, verified research, and practical tips.

Introduce genuinely relevant products or services.

FOR ONLINE COURSE CREATORS

Help subscribers understand the skills they need.
Teach introductory lessons.

Introduce relevant courses and resources.

Give subscribers information they value, then make the next appropriate step easy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 THE TAKEAWAY

An email address isn't a sale.

It's an opportunity to communicate with someone who has chosen to hear from your business.

WHAT IF YOUR BEST CUSTOMER SERVICE STARTED BEFORE THE CUSTOMER EVER HAD A PROBLEM? 🤯

In June 2022, a woman contacted Chewy after her dog died.

She wanted to return unopened dog food.

Chewy refunded her, suggested donating the food, and sent flowers with a personal note.

She shared the experience online.

It went viral, inspiring other customers to share their stories.

Source: Fortune, June 17, 2022.

https://t.co/QzEVMfL0HD

BUT HERE'S WHAT MOST PEOPLE MISS.

The flowers weren't the first thing Chewy did right.

The company made a difficult problem EASY to solve.

The flowers made the experience memorable.

The simple resolution made it useful.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧠 STEP 1: UNDERSTAND THE REAL SECRET TO CUSTOMER LOYALTY

Research covering more than 75,000 customer-service interactions challenged a popular belief.

Customers don't always need extraordinary gestures.

They want problems solved without unnecessary work.

The findings appeared in Harvard Business Review.

"Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers," July–August 2010.

https://t.co/E4k2vS1AYe

What happens after someone pays YOUR business?

Do customers know the next step, what you need, and when work begins?

Will they have to repeat information they've already provided?

Let's teach Grok Bot to predict common problems and prevent them.

Meet your CUSTOMER SUCCESS & RETENTION ENGINE. 🤝

Help first-time buyers become satisfied customers who return and recommend you.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔎 STEP 2: FIND PROBLEMS BEFORE CUSTOMERS EXPERIENCE THEM

Let's use a digital marketing agency as an example.

A customer purchases a website and automation setup.

Your team needs:

• Business, website, and domain details.

• Logo, branding, and existing content.

• Approved services, prices, and FAQs.

• Booking requirements and software access.

• Project decisions and approvals.

What happens if you don't collect these things in advance?

Day 2: You request a logo.

Day 6: You learn the client lacks website access.

Day 9: The booking calendar is missing required details.

Your team loses time, the deadline slips, and the client gets frustrated.

That's a PROCESS problem, not a customer problem.

Grok Bot can collect what's needed before work begins.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📋 STEP 3: CREATE A STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURE

An SOP, or Standard Operating Procedure, documents how to complete a task consistently.

For onboarding:

✅ 1. CONFIRM PURCHASE: Verify payment and package.

✅ 2. WELCOME: Explain the next step.

✅ 3. COLLECT INFO: Use one intake form.

✅ 4. SECURE ACCESS: Use approved invitations or secure sharing.

✅ 5. CHECK READINESS: Verify all requirements.

✅ 6. START WORK: Follow agreed delivery terms.

✅ 7. SEND UPDATES: Report key milestones.

✅ 8. TEST: Verify the finished service.

✅ 9. HAND OFF: Show customers how to use it.

✅ 10. FOLLOW UP: Check that it works for them.

Grok Bot can help implement and manage this repeatable system.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 STEP 4: MAKE IT EASY FOR CUSTOMERS TO HELP YOU HELP THEM

What if clients could finish their setup in ONE session instead of exchanging 15 emails?

Grok Bot can build an intake portal with:

📁 Files and branding.

🌐 Website and domain details.

📅 Booking settings and service FAQs.

✅ Approvals and missing-items checklist.

🔐 Secure access instructions.

Save and reuse their answers throughout the project.

Don't make customers repeat themselves.

Collect only what the work requires.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🤖 STEP 5: TEACH YOUR GROK BOTS TO SUPPORT CUSTOMERS IN YOUR OWN BUSINESS VOICE

Generic chatbots give generic answers.

What if the customer asks, "When will my website be ready?"

Grok Bot should check the actual project record first:

"Your project is in setup.

We have your branding and service details.

We still need booking-calendar access.

Here's the secure link and guide.

Once that's done, we can confirm the next milestone."

A useful answer beats a generic apology.

Never invent a status or delivery date.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📚 STEP 6: BUILD A CUSTOMER SUPPORT KNOWLEDGE BASE

A knowledge base stores approved information used for accurate answers, including:

• Services, packages, prices, and policies.

• Delivery schedules and onboarding steps.

• FAQs and troubleshooting guides.

• Support responsibilities and project records.

• Approved email examples and approval rules.

Keep client records private and separate.

Use verified customer records for personal updates.

If the answer isn't supported, flag it. Don't guess.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

✍️ STEP 7: MAKE THE EMAILS SOUND LIKE YOUR BUSINESS

Train the Bot using approved emails YOU wrote.

Capture your greeting, tone, sentence length, explanations, next steps, and closings.

Have it create a reusable writing guide from those examples.

Keep the warmth and clarity of your business voice, without pretending AI is a human.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🛡️ STEP 8: KNOW WHEN THE BOT SHOULD ASK FOR HELP

Not every email is safe to automate.

Use THREE response levels.

🟢 LEVEL 1: ROUTINE QUESTIONS

Examples: Welcome guides, logo uploads, booking links, package steps.

Answer automatically when authorized, using verified information.

🟡 LEVEL 2: NEEDS VERIFICATION

Examples: Date changes, extra services, design changes.

Research the issue and draft a reply for approval.

🔴 LEVEL 3: HUMAN DECISION REQUIRED

Examples: Refund disputes, contract changes, unauthorized charges, sensitive complaints, privacy or security concerns.

Alert the responsible person with a concise summary.

Internal handoffs needn't interrupt the customer.

But never falsely claim a human wrote an automated reply. Answer truthfully if asked about AI.

If human help is needed, explain the next step without pretending the issue is resolved.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📋 STEP 9: COPY THIS PROMPT INTO YOUR GROK BOT TEAM

📌 COPY FROM HERE:

"@SEO Lead, coordinate a CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SOP & RETENTION SYSTEM for [BUSINESS NAME].

Website: [WEBSITE URL]

Primary service or product: [APPROVED OFFER]

Business platform: [PLATFORM]

CRM: [PLATFORM]

Customer support inbox: [EMAIL OR PLATFORM]

Project management system: [PLATFORM / UNKNOWN]

Use our existing:

• SEO Business Brief.

• Approved Offer & Sales Funnel Report.

• Buyer Voice research.

• Customer email writing guidelines.

• Authorized business policies and project records.

Assign customer communication and response style to Buyer Voice.

Assign forms, portals, knowledge-base integration, and implementation to Website & Content.
