1Introduction
Recently, Large language models (LLM) and agents based on LLM have shown growing promise in clinical medicine, from summarizing patient records and drafting notes to supporting bedside decisions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Now, most medical benchmarks test these models in some closed questions or single-step tasks, such as diagnosis and treatment planning [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. However, clinical care is a multi-step process in which clinicians must adapt their decisions as a patient’s condition and test results evolve. In oncology, for example, patients move from initial diagnosis and treatment planning to toxicity management and long-term surveillance [16, 17, 18]. Moreover, what guides clinical decisions at each stage depends on the specific disease: resectability and operability guide local treatment in non-metastatic lung cancer [19, 20], while cytogenetic and molecular markers inform risk stratification and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia [21, 22]. Because clinical priorities and available evidence shift from one stage to the next, a model that performs well in diagnosis may still fail to adjust treatment appropriately for severe toxicities or monitor for recurrence. This motivates us to design an open-ended disease-specific evaluation organized throughout the care phases to provide a clinically interpretable account of the strengths and limitations of the model in fulfilling the responsibilities in each phase.Recent benchmarks have taken an important step forward by using structured rubrics to assess open-ended medical responses [23, 24, 25]. Rather than relying on a single overall score, these frameworks break clinical expectations down into explicit checkable items, making it much easier to spot missing medical facts, misunderstood patient data, or unsafe advice. For example, HealthBench pairs physician-written rubrics with automated grading to evaluate model behavior in various clinical dialogs [23]. Similarly, Adaptive Precise Boolean rubrics use fine-grained yes-or-no criteria to speed up grading and improve agreement among evaluators in metabolic health [25]. Despite this progress, current rubric-based systems still fall short of real-world clinical demands in two critical ways [23, 25]. First, they evaluate isolated encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities shift across successive decision points for the same patient. Second, they overlook how clinicians phrase their requests differently in daily practice, ranging from broad open-ended questions to highly detailed instructions [23, 5]. Because even subtle changes in wording can sharply alter an LLM’s output [15, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30], testing a model under a single prompt format cannot tell us whether it remains reliable when a busy clinician asks for help in a more general way. Moving beyond static evaluation thus requires solving two connected challenges: how to measure model performance consistently as patients move through distinct stages of care, and how to test whether that performance holds up when the same clinical problem is framed in different https://t.co/JER3ON4scN tackle these challenges, we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a longitudinal benchmark centered on the pathway of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Here, we focus on NPC because its management follows a well-defined, radiotherapy-centered pathway in which each stage demands different clinical reasoning and evidence [31, 32, 33]. Based on clinical semantics, we divide the patient journey into six sequential care phase: Work-up, Diagnosis, Staging, Treatment, Toxicity and Follow-up. Each patient–phase unit is assessed at a defined clinical decision point, with model inputs restricted to evidence available at that time and later information excluded. In each phase, we evaluate model responses using rubrics organised around five shared dimensions: Decision Quality (DQ), Evidence Grounding (EG), Status Determination (SD), Evidence Faithfulness (EF) and Safety Adherence (SA). To ensure scalability, we developed reusable templates within these dimensions to link common clinical requirements to individual patient data. Specifically, these templates capture phase-specific clinical requirements, which are then translated into patient-specific atomic criteria anchored in the clinical evidence available at each decision point. To assess sensitivity to task formulation, we pair each focused, phase-specific clinical request with two variants—a broad clinical request and a detailed prompt specifying expected response components—while keeping the patient–phase unit, underlying clinical evidence and evaluation rubric fixed. Together, these approaches enable consistent comparisons across patients and care phases while providing a modular framework that could be adapted to other cancers and chronic diseases.Following this design, we constructed 941 phase-specific evaluation units and 17,688 case-specific rubric criteria from real-world longitudinal clinical records of 405 patients. With this dataset, we assessed 30 language models and identified distinct performance changes across the care pathway. Although most models demonstrated solid decision quality during initial diagnosis, their reliability dropped sharply in later phases: staging was plagued by explicit decision errors, whereas follow-up suffered from frequent omissions of required clinical actions and evidence. Furthermore, we also found that the performance of some weak models proved to be highly sensitive to task formulation. Specifying the expected elements raised the median quality of decisions, while making the request more general caused a steep drop. This pattern points to a fundamental limitation of current LLMs: they possess substantial medical knowledge, yet may struggle to identify clinical priorities independently without explicit structural guidance. These findings introduce some implications for deploying AI in clinical practice. First, high scores on static diagnostic benchmarks do not guarantee safe performance throughout a patient’s entire treatment journey, since a model that excels at initial diagnosis can still falter during staging or survivorship care. Second, the decline in performance under broad prompts raises concerns about relying on clinical LLMs for autonomous decision-making when busy clinicians ask open-ended questions. Instead, safe clinical integration will require stage-aware guardrails and structured workflow prompts that actively guide models through each phase of care. By identifying where and how models fall short along a longitudinal disease pathway, NPC-RubricBench provides a rigorous foundation for building medical AI systems intended to support patients from their first visit through long-term follow-up.Figure 1:NPC-RubricBench design and composition. a, Longitudinal evaluation setting. Longitudinal records are segmented into six ordered care phases. Patients are counted once across the internal and external cohorts, and each patient–phase unit is counted once. Not every patient contributes every phase. The staging example illustrates uncertainty from a limited biopsy. b, Clinical scenarios. Stacked bars show patient–phase counts across the defined clinical scenarios, using the same inventory as a and a shared absolute-count scale. Definitions and counts are provided in S1.4 and Table S1-B. c, Patient-specific atomic rubrics. Condensed examples illustrate patient-specific criteria for Decision Quality (DQ), Evidence Grounding (EG), Status Determination (SD), Evidence Faithfulness (EF) and Safety Adherence (SA). Schematic outcomes are grouped as Met/Partial/Error/Omission for DQ/EG/SD (upper) and Met/Not met for EF/SA (lower). Partial is permitted only for items with an explicit item-specific partial-credit allowance. Met/Not met denote positive requirements satisfied/unmet, with score factors 1/0. Rubric construction and patient-specific examples are described in S2.1 and S2.3. d, Rubric scale and composition. Annulus sector area encodes rubric-item counts by phase and dimension; n gives phase totals. Counts are of unique patient-specific rubric items. NPC, nasopharyngeal carcinoma; EBV, Epstein–Barr virus; EBER, EBV-encoded RNA; RT, radiotherapy; CCRT, concurrent chemoradiotherapy.

2Results

2.1Benchmark composition and evaluation framework
To construct NPC-RubricBench for evaluating clinical reasoning across successive phases of care, we initially identified 9,153 patients from two clinical centres (9,099 internal and 54 external; dataset inclusion flow, S1.1). Of these, 405 patients were included in the final benchmark, yielding 941 patient–phase evaluation units and 17,688 atomic rubric items (Fig. 1a–d). Each evaluation unit is intentionally structured to link a phase-specific clinical task at a particular decision point with the medical evidence available at that moment. Model responses were subsequently assessed using patient-specific criteria grouped into five shared evaluation dimensions, while clinical scenario labels describe the different clinical contexts represented within each phase.Longitudinal evaluation units. We assembled longitudinal clinical records spanning each patient’s first to most recent documented visit, including clinical notes, laboratory results, physical examination findings, imaging reports and pathology results. We then mapped each patient’s trajectory to six care phases—Work-up, Diagnosis, Staging, Treatment, Toxicity and Follow-up—each representing a distinct clinical responsibility (Fig. 1a). In Work-up, we assessed the examinations and clinical evaluations needed to establish the diagnosis and disease extent; in Diagnosis, the primary pathological diagnosis and other established diagnoses; and in Staging, the T, N and M categories and overall stage. In Treatment, we assessed therapeutic selection and sequencing; in Toxicity, treatment-related adverse events, their management and implications for ongoing treatment; and in Follow-up, post-treatment disease status and surveillance planning. Assessment targets and criterion requirements for all six phases are detailed in Supplementary Section S2.1 (Table S2-A). At selected decision points within these phases, we paired each phase-specific clinical task with the evidence available at that time to form an evaluation unit, excluding later clinical information. Each unit was evaluated separately under the primary Focused formulation. A total of 941 patient–phase units were constructed (784 internal and 157 external), distributed across Work-up (n=191), Diagnosis (n=179), Staging (n=130), Treatment (n=177), Toxicity (n=103) and Follow-up (n=161). To describe the different clinical contexts within each phase, we further grouped the patient–phase units into 17 clinical scenario types (Fig. 1b). Scenario names and corresponding patient–phase counts for the internal and external cohorts are provided in Supplementary Section S1.4 (Table S1-B).Hierarchical rubric framework. To assess these different clinical tasks on the same scale, we organized our rubrics into a three-tier hierarchy: five shared evaluation dimensions, phase-specific clinical targets expressed as reusable templates, and patient-specific atomic criteria (Fig. 1c,d; Supplementary Sections S2.1 and S2.3; Table S1) Specifically, Decision Quality assesses the appropriateness of the final clinical judgement or action. Evidence Grounding examines whether the model identifies and uses key available clinical evidence. Status Determination evaluates whether the model accurately determines the patient’s current clinical state and judges the sufficiency of available evidence for the decision. Evidence Faithfulness checks whether responses introduce claims unsupported by the visible record. Safety Adherence measures compliance with relevant clinical safety constraints. Within each phase and dimension, reusable templates define the core clinical requirements and the patient facts needed to fill them. By populating these templates with the evidence available at each decision point, we generated patient-specific atomic criteria that test individual, independently verifiable clinical requirements. In total, this process produced 17,688 active rubric items (mean, 18.8 per unit), comprising 4,753 items for DQ, 2,773 for EG, 3,069 for SD, 2,880 for EF, and 4,213 for SA. Throughout the care phases, the totals of the items ranged from 1,779 in Toxicity to 3,873 in Treatment (Fig. 1d). Through this hierarchy, the five shared dimensions provide a consistent yardstick across the care pathway, while the instantiated criteria hold the models accountable for the exact clinical facts and constraints of each case.
2.2Model performance across care phases and dimensions
Overall performance and phase-specific differences. Under the primary Focused formulation, we evaluated 30 models on up to 941 eligible patient–phase units from 405 patients in the combined internal and external cohorts. Overall DQ estimates ranged from 29.8 for HuatuoGPT-o1-7B [34] to 85.6 for GPT-5.1 [35] on the 0–100 scale. Overall EF and SA estimates were generally high, ranging from 73.5 to 95.5 and from 77.5 to 97.1, respectively, whereas SD estimates ranged more widely, from 35.1 to 82.5 (Table S2). Across care phases, model-level DQ means ranged from 56.8 to 94.7 during Diagnosis, compared with 8.9 to 56.0 during Staging (Fig. 2a). Model-centred deviations were calculated relative to each model’s equally weighted six-phase mean within the same dimension. All 30 models scored above their own DQ mean during Diagnosis (median deviation +28.0 points) and below it during Staging (−29.3 points). SD showed a similar phase contrast, with positive deviations during Diagnosis in all 30 models (median +22.0 points) and negative deviations during Staging in 29/30 models (−20.5 points). During Work-up, EG and SD were above their respective model-specific means in 30/30 and 27/30 models, with median deviations of +15.7 and +15.3 points. During Treatment, median deviations were positive for DQ (+9.7 points) and SD (+2.0 points), but negative for EG (−5.7 points); these directions were observed in 28/30, 20/30 and 26/30 models, respectively. During Toxicity, all 30 models scored below their own SD mean (median −14.1 points), and 26/30 scored below their EF mean (−7.7 points). Follow-up showed negative median deviations in DQ (−3.7 points), EG (−18.4 points) and SD (−6.9 points), with 26/30, 30/30 and 28/30 models below their respective means. Complete model-centred estimates and direction counts are provided in Tables S7 and S8.Figure 2:Performance across care phases and rubric dimensions. a, Phase-mean distributions. Phase-mean score distributions for 30 models under Focused formulation (text) in the main clinical evaluation set (internal and external cohorts). Scores use dimension-eligible patient–phase units on a bounded 0–100 scale. Violins span observed values; marks show the minimum, median and maximum. Wu, Work-up; Dx, Diagnosis; St, Staging; Tr, Treatment; Tx, Toxicity; Fu, Follow-up. b, Decision quality. DQ means for eight author-selected models, ordered as API-accessed general-purpose, locally deployed open-weight general-purpose and locally deployed open-weight medically adapted groups, with descending overall DQ within each group. c, Evidence grounding. EG means for the same models. d, Status determination. SD means for the same models. Panels b–d share a fixed model order and colours with Figs. 3 and 4c,d; labels are rounded scores. Complete phase-specific scores and denominators are reported in Table S5. DQ, Decision Quality; EG, Evidence Grounding; SD, Status Determination; EF, Evidence Faithfulness; SA, Safety Adherence. Model abbreviations: I, Instruct; T, Thinking/Think. Full names are listed in Table S3.
Model-specific performance. Work-up showed the widest between-model DQ range (12.4–96.7). GPT-5.1 had the highest DQ point estimates during Work-up, Diagnosis, Treatment and Follow-up, whereas Gemini 3.1 [36] had the highest estimate during Staging (56.0) and GPT-5.6-Luna during Toxicity (83.9). Gemini 3.1 also had the highest Staging SD estimate (75.1). Although its overall DQ estimate was slightly higher than that of DeepSeek V4 Pro Think [37] (75.4 versus 74.3), their relative performance differed across phases: Gemini 3.1 scored higher during Work-up (88.1 versus 75.6), but lower during Treatment (69.4 versus 83.7). Model ordering also differed across dimensions within the same phase. During Treatment, Baichuan-M2-32B had higher EG than GPT-5.1 (90.6 versus 82.6), but lower DQ (69.3 versus 94.3) and SD (63.7 versus 89.3). EF showed model-specific low scores despite its generally high overall estimates: Fleming-R1-32B scored 48.2 during Work-up, and Fleming-R1-7B scored 45.0 during Toxicity. Figure 2b–d shows eight selected models, with profiles for all 30 models provided in Suppl. Fig. 1. Complete overall estimates, eligible denominators and patient-cluster bootstrap 95% confidence intervals are provided in Table S2, with phase-specific scores in Table S4 and Table S5. Grouped radars show five-dimensional scores across six phases for the same eight models as Fig. 2b–d and Fig. 4c,d, in API-accessed general-purpose, locally deployed open-weight general-purpose and locally deployed open-weight medically adapted groups. Colours are shared with Fig. 2; outer sectors identify dimensions. b, EF concept violations. EF concept-violation rates: the percentage of resolved, eligible main-evaluation patient–phase units with at least one applicable EF requirement judged Not met. Units with all applicable requirements judged Met remain in the denominator. All phases use one fixed model order. c, SA concept violations. Wu, work-up; Dx, diagnosis; St, staging; Tr, treatment; Tx, toxicity; Fu, follow-up. Panels b,c use full phase names. Model abbreviations: I, Instruct; T, Thinking/Think. A food poster feels more physical when one action breaks the layout.
🍊 one continuous bundle of glossy noodles lifted from the top window, passing through the interface band, and landing in the bowl below
The strands turn three separate zones into one uninterrupted movement.
✨ align chopsticks, suspended noodles, and bowl on one central vertical axis
Your eye travels straight through the graphic card into the food, making the “screen-to-table” idea instantly visible.

GPT- image 2.5 prompt👇
A hyper-real premium food poster advertisement for a fictional noodle brand called SLURPLINE, refined into an Orbit-plus-Transit-plus-Port direction where the original social-post skeleton remains intact, the lifted noodle action becomes more iconic, the flavor system becomes series-ready, and the interface language is reduced into a cleaner curated structure. The composition is a tall vertical social-feed-inspired poster with three zones: an upper food-image window, a middle minimalist interaction-caption band, and a lower real-world bowl zone. The food remains the absolute hero. A pair of dark wooden chopsticks enters from the upper right and lifts a dramatic bundle of glossy fire-kissed chili noodles upward, the strands hanging long, springy, and heavy with believable tension. The noodles pass through the clean interface band and visually connect to the bowl below, making the food feel as if it is escaping the screen into physical space.

Framing and composition: vertical hero poster, strong central axis, clean white social-card borders, top image window occupying the upper third, a reduced minimalist social band in the middle, and a large ceramic bowl anchored in the lower third. Keep the noodle lift as the main visual force line. The chopsticks, suspended noodle bundle, and bowl must align into one clear top-to-bottom movement. Floating garnish elements are fewer but more intentional than before: a few crisp ingredient fragments, herb leaves, and droplets placed in balanced suspension around the lifted strands. Preserve the recognizable social-post architecture, but make it feel more premium, restrained, and design-forward.

Subject design: the noodles are thin, elastic, richly coated, vivid chili-gold, and highly appetizing, with a glossy light oil sheen and subtle steam warmth. Make the flavor direction stronger and more adaptable: the bowl reads as a luxe spicy chili noodle base that can flex toward chili-garlic, sesame tantan, or black garlic heat while keeping the same visual structure. Around the lifted strands, place a few carefully chosen floating cues: one or two caramelized protein slices, one mushroom piece, tiny chopped herbs, and a few crisp fried garnish fragments. The bowl below is a restaurant-grade ceramic bowl with a warm dark glaze, subtle ornamental pattern, white rim and foot, filled with rich amber-red broth, coiled noodles, green vegetables, and restrained toppings. The bowl must feel authentic, premium, and grounded.

Interface and typography: the middle band clearly suggests a social-feed post but is cleaner and more minimal than a literal app screenshot. Use exact visible copy as follows: handle name "SLURPLINE\_KITCHEN", social line "Loved by food people and more", caption text "SLURPLINE\_KITCHEN serve up fire-kissed chili noodles... slurp at your own risk.", and a secondary brand line near the lower-left of the band reading exactly: "SLURPLINE\_KITCHEN est 26". Keep the icon set sparse and elegant, with only essential interaction cues. Typography must be crisp, premium, modern sans-serif, and never compete with the noodles.

Lighting and color: warm commercial food lighting with a soft key from upper left, subtle frontal fill, stronger highlights on the suspended strands, and richer warmth in the broth and bowl. Build clear depth between the bright top image panel, the clean white middle band, and the warm darker lower bowl zone. Palette balance: 60% ivory white, noodle gold, and warm neutral highlights; 30% chili orange, broth amber, and dark ceramic brown; 10% herb green and small red spice accents. Increase contrast so the noodle lift feels more sculptural and the bowl more luxurious, without muddy broth or dirty whites.

Materials and finish: hyper-real food advertising photography fused with polished graphic poster design. Show glossy noodle coating, subtle steam softness, ceramic glaze detail, broth shine, crisp garnish textures, and precise card/interface clarity. The whole finish should feel like a Cannes-level restaurant campaign: craveable, contemporary, smart, and easy to extend into a series.

Output and constraints: premium food poster, product-first hierarchy, no copied source text, no real platform names, no people, no extra props, no chaotic clutter. Keep noodle geometry natural, chopstick grip believable, bowl perspective correct, floating ingredients physically consistent, and typography crisp. Avoid broken strands, malformed noodles, greasy muddy broth, warped bowl perspective, unreadable text, excessive garnish, random utensils, AI gibberish text, dead shadows, or drift away from high-end commercial food realism.

I am always working for unique looking infographics and posters. Here is a prompt I tried for this: 

2x2 grid, 16:9,  AI picks topics Create one finished editorial knowledge poster about the topic below. Make the art-direction decisions yourself, using the topic to determine the composition, hero, supporting elements, and colors. INPUTS TOPIC: [INSERT TOPIC] AUDIENCE: general curious adults ASPECT RATIO: 1:1 TITLE: AUTO HERO CHARACTER OR OBJECT: AUTO LAYOUT: AUTO ACCENT PALETTE: AUTO KEY POINTS AND COUNT: AUTO TAGLINE: AUTO REQUIRED COPY: none Only TOPIC is required. Use the defaults for omitted fields. Any supplied value overrides AUTO. Treat required copy as exact wording. MODULE 1 — CONSISTENT VISUAL STYLE Use oversized black condensed uppercase typography, warm ivory paper, one dominant monochrome illustrated hero, flat geometric color accents, and subtle analog print grain. Combine modernist editorial layout with surreal collage and vintage educational illustration. Use an extreme contrast between the main headline and compact supporting text. Make it feel like part of a thoughtfully designed collectible poster series. MODULE 2 — TOPIC AND COPY Develop a concise, specific 2–5-word title and a memorable 3–8-word tagline suited to the audience. Select a coherent set of approximately 6–12 short, accurate labels about the topic; use fewer if necessary for clarity or accuracy. Choose the appropriate relationship: principles, stages, types, components, or examples. If displaying a count, match it exactly to the visible items. Avoid invented facts, statistics, quotations, and filler. Preserve supplied copy exactly. MODULE 3 — HERO AND VISUAL METAPHOR Choose the single strongest subject for communicating the topic. It may be a human character, animal, plant, machine, artifact, landscape fragment, or surreal hybrid. Choose its pose, direction, crop, expression, and one meaningful exaggeration. Favor a distinctive silhouette and a metaphor connected to how the topic works. Render it in grayscale with sculptural shading, fine stippling or halftone, and crisp collage contours. A human face or oversized eye is optional and should appear only when relevant. MODULE 4 — ADAPTIVE LAYOUT Choose the arrangement around the title length, hero silhouette, and information structure. Freely position the hero and title; place supporting labels in a sidebar, footer, split panel, orbit, or another coherent arrangement. Establish a clear reading order: title, hero, supporting information. Use intentional asymmetry, close alignments, deliberate cropping, and controlled overlap. Protect key facial features, essential object details, and every line of supporting copy. Fit the typography to the format rather than forcing a fixed template. MODULE 5 — GEOMETRY AND PALETTE Choose one primary family of geometric elements that expresses the topic: rays, arcs, ribbons, layers, paths, grids, wedges, or another purposeful form. Use it to connect the hero to the information and guide the eye. Select 2–6 coherent accent colors appropriate to the topic and mood, supported by ivory, black, and grayscale. Keep colors flat, matte, and slightly weathered. Use a rainbow only when conceptually justified. MODULE 6 — FINISH AND QUALITY Make the title dominant and supporting text genuinely readable. Keep paper texture subtle enough to preserve letter clarity. Balance dense focal areas with breathing room. Integrate the text, illustration, and geometric elements into one composition. Avoid generic icon collections, irrelevant decoration, glossy rendering, misspellings, duplicated labels, and accidental text overlaps. If a reference image is attached, use its typography, print texture, tonal contrast, and collage language as style guidance. Let the new topic determine its own layout, character, palette, and motif. Resolve all AUTO choices before rendering. Output one complete poster containing only the intended poster copy. Do not print the input fields, module names, placeholders, or design instructions.

aso 101: what top-ranking apps do differently, after seeing data from 1,000+ apps

After seeing data from 1,000+ apps, the pattern is boring and consistent. The apps that rank treat every metadata field as a separate job and fill each one on purpose. The ones that don't paste the same phrase into all of them and wonder why nothing moves.

Apple publishes most of the rules. Here are 15 steps to actually use them.

1. Give your name one job.
Apple caps the app name at 30 characters. Brand plus your strongest single descriptor, nothing else.
Action: write 5 versions, count the characters, and pick the one a stranger would understand without seeing your icon.

2. Use the subtitle for value, not brand.
The subtitle is also 30 characters and shows under your name across the App Store. Apple says to avoid generic lines like "world's best app."
Action: describe your main use case in the words someone would actually type.

3. Spend all 100 keyword characters.
The keyword field is 100 characters, comma-separated, no spaces after commas. Apple says not to repeat words already in your name, subtitle or category.
Action: delete every keyword that duplicates a word in those three fields and refill the space with new terms.

4. Cut the waste words.
Apple lists what eats space for nothing: plurals of words you already have, the word "app", category names, filler like "the" and "to", and special characters like # or @.
Action: go through your field word by word and remove anything on that list.

5. Mix one popular term with several specific ones.
Apple is blunt about the trade-off: broad terms like "jobs" or "social" bring traffic but are highly competitive, and less common terms bring less traffic with less competition.
Action: if your app is new or small, weight the field toward specific feature terms and keep only one broad term.

6. Keep competitors and trademarks out.
Apple says improper keywords are a common reason for rejection, including trademarked terms, celebrity names, competing app names and irrelevant terms.
Action: remove every competitor and brand name from your keyword field before your next submission.

7. Pick the primary category on purpose.
Apple indexes your primary and optional secondary category in search, and choosing an irrelevant category is grounds for rejection.
Action: set the category your best users would browse, then add a secondary one only if it's genuinely accurate.

8. Design your first 3 screenshots for search.
You get up to 10 screenshots, and the first one to three can show directly in search results when there's no app preview. That's the ad most people actually see.
Action: put your core value in screenshot 1, readable at thumbnail size, and push feature tours to the back.

9. Make the first seconds of your preview count.
You can add up to three app previews of up to 30 seconds each. They autoplay muted on the product page.
Action: open your preview with the payoff, not a logo, and make sure it works with the sound off.

10. Rewrite your first sentence.
Apple calls the first sentence of the description the most important, because it's what people read without tapping "more." It also says not to stuff keywords into the description.
Action: make sentence one a plain statement of what the app does for the user.

11. Keep promotional text for news.
Promotional text is up to 170 characters, sits at the top of the description, and can change any time without a new version. Apple states it does not affect search ranking.
Action: use it for this week's update or offer and keep ranking terms in the keyword field.

12. Treat ratings as a ranking input.
Apple says ratings and reviews influence search ranking. You can prompt up to three times in a 365-day period, and when you reply to a review the reviewer is notified and can update it.
Action: trigger the prompt right after a user's first success, and reply to your recent 1 and 2 star reviews that describe something you've since fixed.

13. Localize, starting with your top markets.
Apple recommends localizing the description, keywords, screenshots and previews per market, and says you can translate the app name and tailor keywords to each market.
Action: pick your top 2 non-English markets and give each its own keyword field, not a translated copy of the English one.

14. Give each search intent its own custom product page.
You can assign keywords to custom product pages so they appear in search instead of your default page. Each keyword combination can only belong to one page.
Action: take your top 2 search intents and build one custom product page for each, with screenshots that match the query.

15. Test the page, then read the numbers.
Product page optimization lets you test alternate icons, screenshots and previews on a share of randomly selected users. App Analytics shows impressions, conversion rate and downloads by source type.
Action: run one screenshot test at a time and filter conversion rate to App Store search to judge it.

Search ranking comes down to two things Apple names: text relevance (name, subtitle, keywords, primary category) and user behavior (downloads, ratings, reviews). Steps 1 to 7 handle the first. Steps 8 to 15 handle the second.

Follow @0xbono for more of these.

10 GitHub projects for better UI design with Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent: components, themes, typography, icons, and motion.

Most component picks are for React apps.

SET THE DESIGN DIRECTION

1. UI/UX Pro Max — give your coding agent design guidance

Have your agent look up palettes, font pairings, and UI guidelines for the kind of product you're building. Useful when every screen seems to drift into a different style.

Requires Python. The MIT-licensed repo covers the basics; Premium features are sold separately.

https://t.co/7Gvqp6xv1F

BUILD THE UI, THEN MAKE IT YOURS

2. shadcn/ui — start with editable components

Forms, dialogs, menus, and other app essentials, with source code you can customize. A starting point for login screens, settings pages, and dashboards. You still choose the layout and visual identity.

https://t.co/yo84JtVO9F

3. tweakcn — change the default shadcn theme

Already using shadcn/ui? Adjust colors, corner radii, and other theme settings in a visual editor, then apply the theme to your project. It changes the styling; page structure and app behavior need their own work.

https://t.co/7MHAmT5u2D

KEEP FONTS AND ICONS CONSISTENT

4. Fontsource — serve fonts from your own site

Choose a font family and the weights you need, then bundle them with your site. Fontsource packages make self-hosting and version management easier. Each font has its own license.

https://t.co/waTqLLXeEV

5. Lucide — use one icon set across the interface

Search, settings, upload, delete: use a consistent set of SVG icons instead of mixing styles. Adjust size, color, and stroke width. Framework packages and standalone SVGs are available.

https://t.co/zckgI0TL3K

ADD MOTION WHERE IT HELPS

6. Magic UI — add a section to your product page

Feature grids, scrolling showcases, animated numbers, and other reusable elements for landing pages. Pick a component that fits your content. The repo is MIT-licensed; Pro templates are paid.

https://t.co/bqgISL2LUP

7. React Bits — give a particular section a visual hook

Browse demos for text animations, backgrounds, and interactive effects, then choose one for the part of the page you want to emphasize. Components come in JavaScript/TypeScript and CSS/Tailwind variants.

Free components use MIT + Commons Clause: personal and commercial projects are allowed, with restrictions on selling or redistributing the components themselves. Pro is separate.

https://t.co/9HhwrOCNL9

Make a panel expand smoothly, animate a reordered list, or add drag interactions. Available for React, JavaScript, and Vue. The core library is MIT-licensed; Motion+ is paid.

HANDLE DATA AND REVIEW THE DETAILS

Build line and bar charts from components for axes, tooltips, and data series. Useful for dashboards. Data fetching, loading states, and empty states are still part of your app's job.

This skill in Vercel's agent-skills repo helps your coding agent review UI code for accessibility and usability, including keyboard navigation, focus states, form feedback, images, typography, and motion. Follow the code review with a browser check of the mobile layout, forms, and buttons.

𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗧𝗢 𝗕𝗨𝗜𝗟𝗗 𝗔𝗡 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 — 𝟴 𝗞𝗘𝗬 𝗦𝗧𝗘𝗣𝗦

Building an AI agent is more than connecting an LLM to a chatbot.

A reliable agent needs the right purpose, tools, memory, orchestration, interface, and testing.

Here’s the complete workflow:

01 — 𝗗𝗘𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗘 𝗣𝗨𝗥𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗘 & 𝗦𝗖𝗢𝗣𝗘

Start with the problem.

→ Define the use case
→ Understand user needs
→ Set success criteria
→ Identify constraints

If you don't know what the agent should accomplish, adding more tools won't fix the problem.

02 — 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗜𝗚𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗬𝗦𝗧𝗘𝗠 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗧

Give the agent clear instructions.

→ Goals
→ Role/persona
→ Instructions
→ Guardrails

The system prompt defines how the agent should behave.

03 — 𝗖𝗛𝗢𝗢𝗦𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗜𝗚𝗛𝗧 𝗟𝗟𝗠

Consider more than just model quality.

→ Base model
→ Context window
→ Parameters
→ Cost
→ Latency

The best model is the one that fits your specific workload.

04 — 𝗔𝗗𝗗 𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗟𝗦 & 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗚𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦

This is where the agent gets real capabilities.

→ APIs
→ Databases
→ MCP servers
→ Custom functions
→ External services
→ Other AI agents

Tools allow the agent to interact with systems beyond the model.

05 — 𝗕𝗨𝗜𝗟𝗗 𝗠𝗘𝗠𝗢𝗥𝗬

Agents often need context beyond a single conversation.

Possible memory systems include:

→ Conversation history
→ Working memory
→ Vector databases
→ SQL databases
→ File storage

Good memory helps the agent maintain relevant context across tasks.

06 — 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗜𝗚𝗡 𝗢𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

Now define how everything works together.

→ Workflows
→ Triggers
→ Parameters
→ Message queues
→ Agent-to-agent communication
→ Error handling

This is what turns individual components into a working system.

07 — 𝗕𝗨𝗜𝗟𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗨𝗦𝗘𝗥 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗘

Give users a practical way to interact with the agent.

→ Chat interface
→ Web app
→ API endpoint
→ Slack/Discord bot

08 — 𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧 & 𝗘𝗩𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗔𝗧𝗘

Never assume the agent works just because the demo works.

Test:

→ Accuracy
→ Quality
→ Latency
→ Tool usage
→ Failure cases
→ Real-world workflows

Then iterate and improve.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘:

𝗣𝘂𝗿𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲 → 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 → 𝗟𝗟𝗠 → 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 → 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 → 𝗢𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲 → 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗞𝗘𝗬 𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡:

A powerful AI agent isn't just a powerful model.

It's a well-designed system where the model, tools, memory, workflows, and guardrails work together.

Save this framework if you're planning to build an AI agent.

Infinity Machine : un agent d’IA à auto-amélioration dédié à la recherche : https://t.co/Cy4QCPqDBu

"arXiv:2610.35579v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 26 Oct 2026
Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
Harish Santhanalakshmi GanesanIndependent researcherharishsg99@gmail.comOctober 2026Abstract
We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent, and use it for research: problems whose answers can be checked by a program or against data. It runs three loops. A discovery loop keeps an archive of scored solutions, and each new candidate is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox, writing and running its own search code and a lab notebook. A catalogue mode searches real data for things nobody has catalogued, judged by a referee rather than a metric. A self-improvement loop lets the system rewrite its own prompts, tools, skills, memory and meta agent behind a gate. An autonomous mode chains everything from a single plain-text goal with no human step: an agent chooses an open problem and writes its verifier; the kernel calibrates that verifier; an adversarial agent audits it; the search runs; an agent that never sees the verifier checks the result; and a final agent writes the report. Proposers see only a public score; where a task has hidden data (held-out instances, later observations), a private split that no agent sees decides what counts. Around this discovery loop the Infinity Machine keeps an editable genome: prompts, tools, skills, an evidence-backed playbook and the meta agent’s own procedure. A kernel that the agent cannot write to gates every change to the genome: it checks policy, compares held-in and held-out performance, and enforces a cost limit. We applied the system to fourteen problems, thirteen of them external, in six days of October 2026, at a total cost of about $180 in model usage. It produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information, each checked by a verifier that the proposing agent did not write:
•an exactly certified point p=0.064966 on the positivity ladder of the qubit depolarizing channel’s quantum capacity (previous certified point 0.064956);
•a single-letter qutrit input that moves that channel’s positivity frontier from the hashing value 0.287087 to 0.2910672;
•a 44-gate, depth-6 Clifford circuit preparing the [[23,1,7]] Golay logical zero, which dominates the published (44,8) and (45,7);
•an exact ten-term stabilizer decomposition showing χ⁡(|T⟩⊗7)≤10 (previously 12).It also cut the added-gate count of the SABRE qubit-routing benchmark from SABRE’s 68,559 to 12,087 (9,312 against the best published 13,044 on the 15 circuits shared with later work), built a 5-parameter transformer that adds 10-digit numbers, closed 24% of the gap between a 20M-parameter language model and the GPT-2 checkpoint on FineWeb validation loss, and surfaced one unconfirmed planet candidate in TESS photometry. In hardware, it redesigned the RTL of an open 8×8 INT8 systolic matrix-multiply tile. Through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow at a fixed clock, it cut the energy per multiply-accumulate from 578.9 fJ to 128.8 fJ (77.7% lower) with 55% less area. Power was measured from gate-level switching activity, and the design stays bit-exact. In three fully autonomous end-to-end runs ($7.59–$9.97 each, no human step after launch), the system chose its problem, wrote and audited its own verifier, searched, and re-checked its result blind. One audit rejected a task whose cited record was stale. All three runs ended in honest ties with the public record, two of them with documented near misses. In one run the agent-written score pointed the wrong way, and none of the checks caught it. We report as carefully the parts that did not work. The system’s one gated attempt to adopt a playbook it had written for itself was rejected on cost. Proposers gamed lenient scorers, usually within a single iteration, four times. And the operator’s hand-made changes to the harness were decisive for several results. We describe them so the reader can separate what the loop did from what its operator did.
1Introduction
Large language models can now write and run substantial programs, and agents built on them can stay on a task for an hour or more. A system that turns this into discoveries needs two things beyond a capable model. It must have a way of telling a real advance from a plausible-looking one, and a way of keeping what it learns. AlphaEvolve [1] and FunSearch [2] show the first. They ground an evolutionary search over programs in automatic evaluation, so that the model’s errors are filtered out by execution, and they reach new results in mathematics and computer science. Work on self-improving agents, including STOP [3], the Darwin Gödel Machine [4], Hyperagents [5] and AIDE2 [6], addresses the second. There the object being evolved is the agent itself, and recursive self-improvement [7] is the long-run aim.The Infinity Machine11Earlier data deposits call the system EVO; the two names refer to the same system. is a research agent that does both. It is not a program-evolution engine with a fixed harness: the unit of work is a researcher-like agent run, the search can be open-ended as well as score-driven, and the harness that directs those agents is itself under gated self-modification. It is built for a single operator with a laptop and a cloud account. Four design choices define it.
1.Agents, not samples. A proposal in the Infinity Machine is a full agent run. A Deep Agents [8] model with a shell, a file system and up to an hour of wall clock in a fresh sandbox reads the task notes and the parent solution. It writes and runs its own search code and delivers a solution together with a lab notebook. A problem therefore receives a handful to about fifteen proposals, not thousands. The proposer, not the harness, decides whether to write a C tableau simulator, an exhaustive enumeration or a gradient ladder.
2.A public/private split. Proposers optimise a public score. Where the task has hidden data, the result is the score on a private split that no agent sees: hidden instances, hidden seeds, or later TESS sectors. For exact-verifier tasks the two splits coincide, and the “private” score is the same verifier rerun by the kernel in its own sandbox. We adopt this split from AIDE2 [6]. It matters because the agents are strong enough to game any scorer they can read (Section 4).
3.The harness is itself an evolvable object. Prompts, tools, skills, the playbook and the meta agent’s procedure form a versioned object, the genome. A meta agent proposes edits to it, and an immutable kernel accepts an edit only if it passes policy, held-in, held-out and cost checks (Section 2.4).
4.End-to-end autonomy with machine-checked trust. The step that usually needs a human, deciding that an agent-written evaluator can be trusted, is replaced by three machine checks: kernel calibration on known cases, an adversarial audit whose exploits the kernel replays, and an independent re-check of the final result by an agent that never sees the evaluator (Section 2.5).
Contributions.
(i) The architecture and its kernel/genome split, the discovery loop with public/private grading, a catalogue mode for open-ended search in real data, the gated self-improvement loop, and an autonomous mode that runs from a plain-text goal to a verified report (Section 2). (ii) Results on fourteen problems (thirteen external): four advances on catalogued open problems in quantum information, a large margin on a widely used compiler benchmark, two machine-learning tasks and one astronomy candidate, with every claim checked by a verifier that was not the agent’s own (Section 3, Table 1). The quantum, SABRE and TESS results are archived with their data and code on Zenodo (DOIs in the bibliography). (iii) Three fully autonomous end-to-end runs, whose safeguards caught a stale record before any search began, and a hardware result: a 77.7% lower energy per MAC for an open accelerator tile, through a full open chip flow with activity-based power (Sections 3.5 and 3.8). (iv) An account of what the self-improvement machinery did and did not achieve, of four specification-gaming incidents, and of the operator’s part in each result (Section 4).
2The Infinity Machine

The kernel owns everything whose corruption would make scores meaningless: scorers, private splits, archive, budget and policy. The genome holds everything the system may change about itself. Agents run inside sandboxes that mount the genome and the public split only.

2.1Kernel and genome
The Infinity Machine is split into an immutable kernel and an editable genome (Figure 1). The kernel contains a daemon that owns long jobs and survives the controlling shell, the archive (the genome’s version history as a lineage DAG, with rollback), the scorers, the gate, the strategy and model bandits, reward logging, and the budget middleware. The genome contains the task agent’s and meta agent’s prompts, the meta agent’s procedure and weakness-mining script, tools with tests, skills with fixtures, and an ID-addressed playbook in which every bullet carries evidence run IDs and a confidence. The split follows the rule from harness-engineering practice [9]: whatever the agent may legitimately want to change is in the genome, and whatever would let it change its own grade is not. The kernel never trusts an agent’s report of what it ran. It records tool calls itself, and scorers read solutions produced in a fresh sandbox.
2.2Task specification
A task consists of a specification (problem family, description, scorer, score range and direction, sandbox image and resources, per-run budget, and a brief), a public split (problem statement, notes, tools, a local verifier), a private split and an optional seed solution. The scorer is either a verifier program that the kernel runs in its own sandbox, whose value is mapped linearly onto [0,1], a test suite, or a retrain-from-code scorer for ML tasks. The brief is the operator’s channel to the proposers: it lists what has already been measured and what to try.experience bank(all solutions, public & private scores)parent sampling∝σ⁡(λ⁡(spub−s¯top3))1+#​childrenstrategy arm(UCB1 per family)P proposer agents in parallel, each in a fresh sandbox, ≤1 h, per-run $ capsolution/ + NOTES.md+ search codekernel scorespublic → selectionprivate → resultbrief + parent +bank summary(public only)addFigure 2:One iteration of the discovery loop. Private scores never reach an agent. In catalogue mode every proposer extends the shared merged catalogue instead of a sampled parent, and the referee’s per-claim verdicts are passed on as feedback.

2.3Discovery loop
A discovery session runs N iterations of the loop of Figure 2 with P proposers each. The kernel scores the seed and places it in an experience bank. In each iteration it samples P parents with probability proportional to σ⁡(10​(spub−s¯))/(1+c). Here spub is the parent’s public score, s¯ is the mean public score of the top three entries and c is the parent’s number of children. This is the DGM/Hyra rule [4, 10], which favours good parents that have not been expanded much. Each proposer also receives a named strategy, drawn by a per-family UCB1 bandit whose reward is whether the child beat its parent on the public score; AIDE2 [6] found UCB over named strategies to be its most valuable discovered mechanism. The default arms, written for the optimisation family and used by every family without its own set, are conservative, aggressive rewrite, new neighbourhood, data structure and robust/simple. Math tasks use structured construction, exhaustive small case, new objective, scale compute and literature transfer. ML tasks use new architecture family, parameter sharing, embedding budget, connectivity and recipe; astronomy tasks have five search-oriented arms of their own.A proposer is a fresh Deep Agents model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) in a sandbox that mounts the genome, the task’s public split and an inspiration folder: the parent solution and a bank summary that shows public scores only. It works with a shell for up to about an hour. It must keep its solution directory current, because a per-run spend cap ($4 by default), checked before every model call, can end it at any turn. On return, the kernel scores the solution on both splits in a separate sandbox, appends it to the bank and logs the strategy reward. The session’s answer is the best public solution, and its private score is what we report.
Catalogue mode.
Optimisation has a parent to improve; open-ended discovery in real data does not. A task in catalogue mode changes the deliverable to a list of claims plus a search log. The scorer becomes a referee, which re-measures every claim from the raw data, checks it against catalogues of known objects and returns per-claim verdicts. Those verdicts reach the next proposer as feedback. The hidden split is prediction: for the TESS task, the private verifier mounts later observing sectors that no agent can read and checks whether each periodic claim predicts dips there. After each round the kernel merges all accepted claims into one shared catalogue, which every proposer then extends.
2.4Self-improvement loop
The self-improvement loop improves the genome rather than a solution. A UCB or score-child selector picks a parent generation. The meta agent (Claude Opus 5.5), whose prompt and procedure are themselves genome files [5], reads an evidence bundle of recent runs and mines weaknesses. It proposes one bounded edit together with a manifest that states the evidence, the root cause and the predicted fixes. The kernel then applies a static policy check (only genome paths may change, kernel-owned files are byte-identical, at most 12 files) and grades the candidate on held-in and held-out tasks. It accepts the candidate only if neither split regresses beyond a noise band of 0.03 and the cost is at most 1.5 times the incumbent’s. A gain larger than 0.3 is parked for human review instead of being activated. Predictions in the manifest are checked against per-task deltas, and a meta agent whose predictions keep failing is sampled less often.Three further paths feed the genome. Consolidation [11] reflects on run records and edits playbook bullets by ID. Bullets that a run retrieved are confirmed or weakened by that run’s outcome, and recurring lessons are promoted to skills, which must pass a fixture. Capability requests let a task agent ask for a tool; a toolsmith subagent writes it with tests, and the kernel re-runs those tests before the requester may use the tool. Rewards come from scores and from the operator’s good/bad feedback on individual runs, and update the bandits and playbook confidence. Every path ends in a generation that passes the same gate, so every self-modification is auditable and reversible.
2.5Autonomous mode: from a goal to a verified report
In the modes above a human writes the task: the problem statement, the verifier, the seed and the notes. Autonomous mode removes that step. Its only input is a plain-text research goal; the default goal asks for an open problem whose best known result is an explicit object or number that a program can check exactly. Every phase is an agent run in its own fresh sandbox, and the kernel only validates, routes and records (Figure 3).
1.Scout (network on). The scout surveys public problem catalogues and the literature, picks one problem, and checks that it is still open. It writes a complete task to a fixed contract: a task specification with the record and its source, a problem statement, a verifier program, a seed solution, at least four calibration cases with known outcomes (valid ones with their exact values, invalid ones that must be rejected), and a selection note with the evidence of openness.
2.Kernel validation. The kernel runs the verifier on the seed and on every calibration case in a network-off sandbox. Valid cases must reproduce their stated values, and invalid cases must be rejected or score no better than the seed. The scoring range must also extend beyond the record, so that beating the record registers.
3.Adversarial audit (network on). A fresh agent re-checks that the problem is open and the record current, and tries to construct invalid solutions that the verifier accepts at or above the record. The kernel replays every exploit file through the verifier. The audit fails if the auditor says so or if any exploit is accepted. Its findings go back to the scout for a repair round (at most three rounds).
4.Installation. The task is installed and the approval is recorded as automatic, with its basis (calibration, audit and exploit replay). This replaces the human approval that an agent-proposed evaluator otherwise requires.
5.Discovery. The ordinary loop of Section 2.3 runs on the generated task.
6.Independent check (network off). A fresh agent receives only the problem statement and the best solution, never the verifier. It writes its own checker, tests it on cases it constructs, and evaluates the solution. The kernel compares the two values.

2.6Infrastructure and the operator
Sandboxes are local Docker containers (network off, read-only root, no kernel files, no private split) or Modal sandboxes behind the same interface. Modal provides GPU (one H100) and read-only data volumes for the ML and astronomy tasks. A daemon owns sessions, so a closed terminal does not kill a run, provided the session is submitted as a daemon job; one session started from a foreground shell lost a proposer run when that shell died (Section 4).The fourteen problem campaigns of Sections 3.1–3.7 were run before autonomous mode existed, and in them the operator’s role was substantial. The accelerator campaign (Section 3.5) ran later, in the same operator-led way. We want to be exact about it. For each of those problems the operator, working with an AI coding assistant:
•chose and vetted the problem against the literature;
•wrote the verifier, seed and task notes;
•launched the sessions;
•gave run-level feedback;
•after each session, updated the notes with an “already measured” table, which was the main channel by which one session learned from the last;
•fixed kernel bugs;
•re-verified and certified every result on the host, and wrote and deposited the notes.The operator also wrote family-specific strategy arms by hand three times (math and ML after observing failures, and astronomy when adding catalogue mode). Under our own rules that is a kernel change rather than a genome change, but it shaped later results, and we discuss it in Section 4. In the three autonomous runs (Section 3.8) the operator’s only actions were writing the goal text and launching the job: an agent chose the problem and wrote the task, and the kernel and other agents did everything up to and including the report.

👇prompt

Create a premium Japanese brand design system board based on:

[THEME] {例：デザインだけじゃ足りない時代。仕事と双子育児の合間にあれこれ試して「これは！」と思えたものをお届け｜プロのアートディレクター目線の遊び心のあるデザイン・写真、ブランドカラー蛍光ピンク}

[BRAND NAME] {例：MIYAMA creative}

Aspect ratio: 4:5
Language: Japanese

You are a top-tier creative director, art director, brand designer, graphic designer, UI/UX designer and typographer.

First interpret THEME and TARGET, then automatically determine the most appropriate brand personality, color palette, typography, imagery, information density, shapes, spacing and visual tone.

Do NOT apply the same style to every theme.
Creative brands may feel editorial and expressive; technology may feel intelligent and precise; beauty may feel elegant and sensorial; B2B may feel refined and trustworthy; family-oriented brands may feel warm and approachable.
Always choose the art direction that best fits the actual theme and audience.

The result must feel like a high-budget Japanese advertising agency or elite branding studio created a complete brand identity and digital design system.

Create one polished Figma / Behance-style showcase board with an asymmetric modular composition, generous whitespace, consistent spacing and sophisticated rounded panels.

Place ONE large realistic smartphone mockup at the visual center.
Use natural modern smartphone proportions around 19.5:9. Never make it excessively tall, thin or stretched.

Around the smartphone, compose approximately 8–12 varied modules including:

- large desktop website hero
- brand logo / wordmark
- 5–7 color palette
- Japanese typography specimen
- 3 project / service cards
- buttons, inputs, checkbox, toggle and other UI components
- icon set
- tags / chips
- news or content list
- expressive CTA card
- website footer

The desktop hero and smartphone must show convincing real website designs, not posters placed inside frames.

Build one coherent visual system across every module.
Repeat 3–5 distinctive brand devices such as characteristic shapes, corner radius, icon geometry, typography treatment, color blocks, illustration style or symbolic motifs.

Typography is especially important.
Use professional Japanese typography with strong hierarchy, beautiful line breaks, controlled spacing and a clear contrast between large headlines and small supporting text.
Prefer less text over unreadable or meaningless text.

Use photography, illustration, mascot, abstract graphics or objects only when appropriate to THEME.
They must feel custom art-directed for the brand, never like random stock assets.

Color must be intentional and controlled:
one dominant foundation + primary brand color + secondary color + limited accents.
Avoid random rainbow palettes, muddy colors and generic AI blue-purple gradients unless conceptually appropriate.

Aim for:
high-budget Japanese advertising,
premium brand identity,
award-level art direction,
polished digital product design,
excellent typography,
strong visual hierarchy,
commercially realistic production quality.

Avoid:
generic SaaS UI,
plain equal-sized grids,
cheap template aesthetics,
excessive shadows or glassmorphism,
random blobs,
inconsistent colors or corner radii,
tiny illegible text,
fake statistics or awards,
unnecessary charts or QR codes,
multiple competing smartphones,
visual clutter.

Do not maximize information.
Maximize art direction, hierarchy and brand coherence.

The final image should instantly communicate:
“This is a complete brand world designed from one strong system.”

Keep the image rich but controlled, never chaotic.

Lighting uses a high-impact golden-hour palette with warm-to-cool contrast. Palette hierarchy: 60% sunset gold, amber, cola brown, and glowing warm highlights; 30% deep marine blue, twilight teal, and coastal shadow tones; 10% vivid red brand accents and off-white typography. Main light comes from the sun behind and slightly behind the bottle, creating luminous transmission through the cola, glowing edge highlights, and warm reflections on glass and water. Add soft frontal fill to preserve label readability. The open bottle mouth should catch a subtle specular rim and hint of inner glass thickness. Avoid muddy shadows, dead blacks, or oversaturated tourist colors. The emotional tone is joyful, nostalgic, expansive, and premium.

Materials must feel hyperreal and polished: convincing glass thickness, condensation droplets, subtle label fiber texture, rich internal liquid refraction, a precise cold uncapped rim with wet highlights and believable glass lip detail, a glossy floating cap with slight edge wear, and small but believable island textures such as stone edge, foliage, wood decking, painted kiosk surfaces, van trim, and water foam at the shoreline. The red liquid ribbon should feel like a hybrid of real splash physics and design gesture, glossy, aerodynamic, and visually clean. Keep hero zones extremely crisp and the distant background elegantly soft.

Integrate original English typography as an essential graphic layer. Beneath it, add a smaller support block such as “this season, make every hour glow a little longer.” At the top right, place a tiny lifestyle triplet line like “SIP • SHARE • STAY”. At the lower left, add three compact circular icon-style markers with short descriptors such as “bright refreshment”, “timeless spark”, “made to gather”. At the lower right, place a concise emotional closing line such as “one bottle, endless warm moments.” Add a subtle hashtag or campaign cue near the bottom only if needed. Typography must feel art-directed, balanced, and kept away from the bottle recognition zone.

Output: a full-bleed premium beverage poster with product-first hierarchy, strong campaign readability, cinematic micro-world storytelling, clean graphic order, hyperreal bottle detail, open bottle mouth clearly visible, one single floating cap in the air, no cap attached to the bottle, no real brand names, no copied slogans, no extra oversized bottles, no warped glass shape, no unreadable text, no chaotic crowding, no muddy sunset haze, no dead black areas, no low-quality AI textures, no generic stock-ad feeling, no off-brand packaging, no style drift, and no clutter competing with the hero bottle.

2114503106142540182.text:
Someone asked me what good approaches there are for developing with AI right now. I said it mainly depends on how far you are using AI, and whether it is a new project or maintaining an old project. If this were really expanded on, it would be a very large amount of content. But briefly, from my personal experience, there are a few points:

1. Requirements and detailed design can be done by AI, but the architecture must be reviewed and controlled by you personally.

2. There must be four core constraints. The first is to require documents and conversations to speak in plain human language. The second is that any creation or rewriting of documents must not compress any information, and must not be oriented toward saving tokens. The third is that code must have comments: any function, class, interface, and important logic must have comments. These three points, to put it plainly, solve the problem of whether you can understand your documents and whether you can understand your code. The last one is to reuse existing code whenever you can, and if there is a mature open-source project or third-party library, use it. Do not reinvent the wheel. This is also very important. Otherwise you will find that the AI has written a large amount of code, which in practice is not as useful as one mature library.

3. The first batch of documents written by AI must be read carefully. Even if you feel very impatient reading them, read them carefully anyway, and try to solve as many problems as possible at the document stage. Otherwise, as the AI writes more and more code and more and more documents, you will become less and less willing to read documents and less willing to read code. A lot of drift and scope expansion comes from this point.

4. In the requirements, architecture, and design stages, the interview style is very useful. You can have the agent use an interview-style approach to write together with you, or you can have the agent and sub-agents ask and answer questions among themselves as a substitute for you. But every step must be appended to a list. Do not trust that its context compression mechanism is good enough.

5. Unit tests and quality gates are needed, especially as the project gets bigger. But the rules must be set properly: one is the timing for writing and using unit tests and gates, and the other is not to run the full suite every time. This can decide the development speed and the waste of tokens, while also avoiding falling into the premature optimization swamp too early.

6. Whether one agent writes your project or multiple sub-agents develop in parallel, one very obvious problem appears: duplicate code and duplicate logic. This is currently hard to avoid, even if you have written constraints like in my point 2. The Ponytail skill library has a certain effect, but you cannot use the original version. It has to be modified, otherwise the effect will not be very good. Looking across the whole project, there will still be a large amount of code that could have been merged or abstracted, but in fact exists in multiple written versions. And if it is used improperly, it will cause problems with your code quality.

7. Review is a must, no matter the size of each task, and the review must be independent and strict. What does independent mean? It means the developer does not review its own work. Hand it to other sub-agents, and if conditions allow, even hand it to a different large model. Reviews generally need to go through multiple rounds, depending on complexity. For something simple, one agent reviews it. For something complex, multiple agents review from different angles, or are assigned different modules to review, and then the main agent is responsible for deduplication, cross-verification, and the final investigation. This step is very important, because many issues require cross-verification to find the root cause. Otherwise it becomes patch-style development over and over: the fix only solves the symptom, not the cause. You have it fix something, then review again and new problems appear. After multiple rounds you have fixed a big pile of things, but the root cause might actually be only one. Another point is to watch whether the review is over-reviewing. You can write prompts for this, or write a skill yourself, but in the end it still relies on your own ability. No prompt or skill can guarantee that over-reviewing will not happen. Finally, do not just say "review this for me" and be done with it. Point out the aspects to focus on. For example: review whether there are memory problems such as out-of-bounds access, overflow, or leaks; whether there is over-design; whether thread ownership and the use of async threads are correct, and so on.

8. On the use of skills, I do not recommend enabling strongly constraining skill packs like Superpowers on the current top-tier models. These do have an effect, but the benefit is not necessarily that large. Personally, the built-in skills plus a few I have modified myself are enough. For a team, one or two engineered skills are enough. Any more than that becomes a burden. To put it in plain words, even if you use TDD, DDD and all that stuff, the output is still reviewed by AI in practice. The bigger the project, the harder human review becomes.

9. The most important thing is that even if your project runs tens of thousands of gates and passes them all, it does not mean your project can go live. This itself is a false proposition. Because no matter how many gates there are, and no matter how complete the unit test coverage is, it does not mean the project itself will not have problems. At most, these guarantee that under limited, already verified preconditions, the project is fine. As for how to do it, every company has its own way. For example, on one small project of ours, the full gate suite has over 100,000 checks and takes 30 minutes to run once. But we still had another agent rewrite a set of attack programs based on the design documents, and added it as the final stage of CI.

10. There are some other techniques that many people online have already talked about. For example, AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md should contain no more than 100 lines of core instructions, and everything else should only serve as an index. Internal documents should be stored in a structured directory, with an entry index in each directory. Tests should have a ledger, and every test run must be appended to the ledger. Document management should not rely on numbering, but on the git repository. And so on. I will not say more about these; they are everywhere online.

11. Oh, I almost forgot, there is also the selection of large models. I do not know domestic (Chinese) models very well, and I have basically never used them. Just from Claude and GPT, they are suitable for different fields. Claude's analytical ability is very strong. It performs very well in the architecture and design stages of a project, much better than GPT. Its only real downside is that its autonomy is too strong. If you do not constrain it well, it will do a lot of unnecessary things for you. GPT is indeed much worse than Claude at solving complex problems, but it is more obedient when it comes to doing the work, so it depends on how you use them. I generally give complex problems to Claude, and simple, local code writing to GPT. Also, a lot of the time I use Claude to direct GPT to do the work. This works quite well. In Claude Code, it supervises GPT doing the specific tasks, and corrects and adjusts in time. As for model switching, I do not recommend switching back and forth the way people online suggest, like using the strongest model for analysis first, and a second-tier model for doing the work. A continuous task is best not switched back and forth, unless it is inherently a main task and sub-tasks. This is not a context problem, it is a problem of the large model's own cache hits.

There is more that I either cannot recall at the moment, or that needs proper expansion to explain. In short, the above is a brief summary of some of my experience. If it were really expanded, this would be a very large body of content, not something a few points can make clear. You happened to ask, so I briefly shared my experience. Since this was off the cuff, some of it may be incomplete or incorrect. For reference only.
